Single long sentences that introduce several symbols and also state results or constructions; kept whole since nodes never split a sentence.

nodes.name: Data and data generating distribution
nodes.statement: Consider a situation where we observe a data set $y\in{\mathbb R}^{n\times\ell}$ that is a realization of an unknown probability distribution ${\mathbb P}_n$ on the Borel sets of the sample space ${\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}$.

nodes.name: Rows of the data and marginal distributions
nodes.statement: We denote the $i$-th row of the data vector (matrix) $y$ by $y_i\in{\mathbb R}^{1\times \ell}$, so that $y=(y_1',\dots, y_n')'$, and write ${\mathbb P}_{i,n}$ for the marginal distribution corresponding to that row.

nodes.name: Product form of the data generating distribution
nodes.statement: Throughout, we assume that the data generating distribution is of product form, that is ${\mathbb P}_n = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n {\mathbb P}_{i,n}$.

nodes.name: Candidate set of models
nodes.statement: Suppose further that one wants to conduct inference on $\mathbb{P}_n$, and intends to use as a working model an element of $\mathsf{M}_n$, a set consisting of $d$ nonempty sets of distributions $\mathbb{M}_{1,n}, \hdots,\mathbb{M}_{d,n}$ on the Borel sets of ${\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}$.
nodes.genus: a set consisting of $d$ nonempty sets of distributions

nodes.name: Model-specific target of inference
nodes.statement: For each model $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ one has to define a corresponding target of inference $\theta^*_{\mathbb{M},n} = \theta^*_{\mathbb{M},n}(\mathbb{P}_n)$, say, which we take as given throughout the present section.

nodes.name: Dimension of the target
nodes.statement: Furthermore we assume that for every $\mathbb{M}_{j,n} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ the target is an element of a Euclidean space of finite dimension $m(\mathbb{M}_{j,n})$ which does not depend on $n$.

nodes.name: Model selection procedure
nodes.statement: We take a model selection procedure as given, and denote the model selection procedure used by $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to \mathsf{M}_n$ (measurable). That is, the quantity $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n(y)$ denotes the selected model upon observing $y$.

nodes.name: Model-specific estimator
nodes.statement: We also assume that for every model $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ an estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\mathbb{M},n}: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb{M})}$ (measurable) of the corresponding target $\theta^*_{\mathbb{M},n}$ is available.

nodes.name: POSI approach to confidence intervals post-model-selection
nodes.statement: Our approach is as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, we construct confidence intervals $\mathrm{\mathrm{CI}}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}$ for the $j$-th component $\theta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*(j)}$ of $\theta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*}$, for every $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ and every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ so that \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \in \mathrm{CI}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M}) \text{ and all } \mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n \right) \end{equation*} is not smaller than $1-\alpha$. \item For a model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb M}_n$, our suggested confidence intervals are then obtained via \begin{equation*} \mathrm{\mathrm{CI}}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \text{ for } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n). \end{equation*} From the coverage property in Part~1 we obtain \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Build intervals covering all coordinates of all candidate-model targets simultaneously, then report those of the selected model.

nodes.name: Simultaneous intervals over all models
nodes.statement: Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, we construct confidence intervals $\mathrm{\mathrm{CI}}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}$ for the $j$-th component $\theta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*(j)}$ of $\theta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*}$, for every $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ and every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ so that \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \in \mathrm{CI}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M}) \text{ and all } \mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n \right) \end{equation*} is not smaller than $1-\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct intervals with asymptotic simultaneous coverage $1-\alpha$ over all models and coordinates.

nodes.name: Report intervals of the selected model
nodes.statement: For a model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb M}_n$, our suggested confidence intervals are then obtained via \begin{equation*} \mathrm{\mathrm{CI}}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \text{ for } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n). \end{equation*} From the coverage property in Part~1 we obtain \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}^{(j)}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Use the intervals of the selected model; coverage follows from Part 1.

nodes.name: Set of admissible distributions $\mathbf{P}_n$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathbb{P}_n$, the distribution that generated the data $y$, is known to be an element of a set $\mathbf{P}_n$. The set $\mathbf{P}_n$ describes the assumptions one is willing to impose on the unknown distribution in a particular modeling scenario, and will typically be large and potentially nonparametric.

nodes.name: Normal distribution notation
nodes.statement: A normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and (possibly singular) covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is denoted by $N(\mu, \Sigma)$.

nodes.name: POSI constant $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$
nodes.statement: For $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and a covariance matrix $\Gamma$ we denote by $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$ the $1-\alpha$-quantile of the distribution of the supremum-norm $\|Z\|_{\infty}$ of $Z \sim N(0, \Gamma)$.
differentia: of the distribution of the supremum-norm $\|Z\|_{\infty}$ of $Z \sim N(0, \Gamma)$

nodes.name: Correlation matrix, Moore-Penrose inverse and matrix square roots
nodes.statement: The correlation matrix corresponding to a covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is denoted by $\mathrm{corr}(\Sigma) = \mathrm{diag}(\Sigma)^{\dagger/2} \Sigma \mathrm{diag}(\Sigma)^{\dagger/2}$, where $\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma)$ denotes the diagonal matrix obtained from $\Sigma$ by setting all off-diagonal elements equal to $0$, $A^{\dagger}$ denotes the Moore-Penrose inverse of the quadratic matrix $A$, $A^{1/2}$ denotes the symmetric non-negative definite square root of the non-negative definite matrix $A$, and where we abbreviate $[A^{\dagger}]^{1/2}$ by $A^{\dagger/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: corr$(\Sigma)$ rescales $\Sigma$ by its diagonal via the Moore-Penrose square root.

nodes.name: Extreme eigenvalues
nodes.statement: The smallest and largest eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix $A$ is denoted by $\lambda_{\min}(A)$ and $\lambda_{\max}(A)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Diagonal matrix of a vector
nodes.statement: For a vector $v$ with coordinates $v^{(1)}, \hdots, v^{(l)}$ we also use the symbol $\mathrm{diag}(v)$ to denote the diagonal matrix with first diagonal entry $v^{(1)}$, second $v^{(2)}$, and so on.

nodes.name: Operator and Euclidean norms
nodes.statement: The operator norm of a matrix $A$ (w.r.t. the Euclidean norm) is denoted by $\|A\|$, and the Euclidean norm of a vector $v$ is denoted by $\|v\|$.

nodes.name: Diagonal entry abbreviation
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $A_{ii}$, the $i$-th diagonal element of a quadratic matrix $A$, is occasionally abbreviated as $A_i$.

nodes.name: Indicator identification
nodes.statement: We also identify the indicator function $\mathbbm{1}_B$ of a set $B$ with the set $B$ itself, whenever there is no risk of confusion.

nodes.name: Weak convergence notation
nodes.statement: Weak convergence of a sequence of probability measures $\mathbb{Q}_n$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{Q}_n \Rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Image measure notation
nodes.statement: The image measure induced by a random variable (or vector) $x$ defined on a probability space $(F, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{Q})$ is denoted by $\mathbb{Q} \circ x$.

nodes.name: Holds eventually
nodes.statement: For a sequence $(a_n)_{n\in{\mathbb N}}$, we say that a property \emph{holds eventually} if there exists a positive integer $n_0$ such that the property holds for every $a_n$ with $n\ge n_0$.

nodes.name: Expectation and variance operators
nodes.statement: The expectation operator and the variance-covariance operator w.r.t. $\mathbb{P}_n$ is denoted by $\mathbb{E}_n$ and $\mathbb{V}_n$, respectively; and the expectation operator and the variance-covariance operator w.r.t. $\mathbb{P}_{i,n}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{E}_{i,n}$ and $\mathbb{V}_{i,n}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Stacked estimators and targets
nodes.statement: Our methods for constructing uniformly valid confidence intervals post-model-selection are developed under a high-level condition imposed on the stacked vector of estimators $\hat{\theta}_n = (\hat{\theta}_{\mathbb{M}_1, n}', \hdots, \hat{\theta}_{\mathbb{M}_d, n}')'$ centered at the corresponding stacked vector of targets $\theta_n^* = (\theta^{*'}_{\mathbb{M}_1, n}, \hdots, \theta^{*'}_{\mathbb{M}_d, n})'$.

nodes.name: Total dimension $k$
nodes.statement: In this section we denote the dimension of $\hat{\theta}_n$ by $$k \quad := \quad \sum_{j = 1}^d m(\mathbb{M}_{j,n}),$$ which does not depend on $n$.

nodes.name: Condition 1 (asymptotically linear representation)
nodes.statement: There exist Borel measurable functions $g_{i,n}: {\mathbb R}^{1 \times \ell}\to {\mathbb R}^k$ for $i = 1, \hdots, n$, and $\Delta_n:{\mathbb R}^{n\times \ell}\to{\mathbb R}^k$, possibly depending on $\theta^*_n$, so that for $y\in{\mathbb R}^{n\times \ell}$ \begin{equation} \hat{\theta}_n(y) - \theta_n^* \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n g_{i,n}(y_i) + \Delta_n(y), \end{equation} where, writing $r_n(y) := \sum_{i = 1}^n g_{i,n}(y_i)$, it holds for every $i \in \{1, \hdots, n\}$ and every $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{i,n}\left(g^{(j)}_{i,n}\right) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad 0 < \mathbb{V}_{n}\left(r_n^{(j)} \right) < \infty. \end{equation} Furthermore, for every coordinate $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ we have \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{V}_n^{-1}\left(r^{(j)}_n\right)\sum_{i = 1}^n \int_{{\mathbb R}^{1 \times \ell}} \left[g^{(j)}_{i, n}\right]^2 \left\{|g^{(j)}_{i, n}| \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}^{\frac{1}{2}}_n(r^{(j)}_n) \right\} d\mathbb{P}_{i,n} \to 0 \\ &\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} and \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \big|\mathbb{V}^{-1/2}_{n}\left(r_n^{(j)} \right) \Delta_n^{(j)} \big| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Estimation error = sum of independent centered summands plus negligible remainder, with marginal Lindeberg conditions.
nodes.label: cond:sum

nodes.name: Equation (2.1) [eq:repres]
nodes.statement: \hat{\theta}_n(y) - \theta_n^* \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n g_{i,n}(y_i) + \Delta_n(y),
nodes.label: eq:repres

nodes.name: Equation (2.2) [eq:mom]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}_{i,n}\left(g^{(j)}_{i,n}\right) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad 0 < \mathbb{V}_{n}\left(r_n^{(j)} \right) < \infty.
nodes.label: eq:mom

nodes.name: Equation (2.3) [eq:linde]
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{V}_n^{-1}\left(r^{(j)}_n\right)\sum_{i = 1}^n \int_{{\mathbb R}^{1 \times \ell}} \left[g^{(j)}_{i, n}\right]^2 \left\{|g^{(j)}_{i, n}| \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}^{\frac{1}{2}}_n(r^{(j)}_n) \right\} d\mathbb{P}_{i,n} \to 0 \\ &\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0, \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:linde

nodes.name: Remark: $g_{i,n}$ as functions on the full sample space
nodes.statement: The careful reader will have noticed, that the functions $g_{i,n}:{\mathbb R}^{1\times\ell}\to{\mathbb R}^k$ in Condition~\ref{cond:sum} do not depend on all of the observation matrix $y\in{\mathbb R}^{n\times\ell}$, but only on its $i$-th row $y_i\in{\mathbb R}^{1\times\ell}$. This is crucial. In the sequel, however, it will be convenient to also consider $g_{i,n}$ as a function on the full sample space ${\mathbb R}^{n\times \ell}$. Thus, we sometimes identify $g_{i,n}$ with the composition $g_{i,n}\circ\pi_{i,n} : {\mathbb R}^{n\times \ell}\to {\mathbb R}^k$, where $\pi_{i,n}:{\mathbb R}^{n\times\ell}\to{\mathbb R}^{1\times\ell}$ is the coordinate projection $\pi_{i,n}(y) = y_i$.
nodes.label: rem:gin

nodes.name: Equation (2.4) [eqn:distresc]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right].
nodes.label: eqn:distresc

nodes.name: Distance metrizing weak convergence
nodes.statement: Here $d_w$ denotes a distance metrizing weak convergence of probability measures on the Borel sets of the respective Euclidean space the dimension of which is not shown in the notation (cf. the discussion in \cite{dudleyreal} pp. 393 for specific examples).

nodes.name: Matrix $S_n$ of outer products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, in the second part of Lemma~\ref{lemma:equivSn}, defining under Condition~\ref{cond:sum} the matrix \begin{equation} S_n(y) := \sum_{i = 1}^n g_{i,n}(y_i) g'_{i,n}(y_i), \end{equation} we show that a suitable approximation statement continues to hold if $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$ is replaced by $S_n$: the $d_w$-distance between \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right], \end{equation} and the sequence of (random) Gaussian distributions $N\left(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n)\right)$ converges to $0$ in ${\mathbb P}_n$-probability as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $S_n=\sum_i g_{i,n}g_{i,n}'$; Gaussian approximation persists with $S_n$ in place of $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.6) [eqn:distresc2]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right],
nodes.label: eqn:distresc2

nodes.name: Gaussian approximation of the rescaled estimation error
nodes.statement: Under Condition \ref{cond:sum} \begin{equation*} d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N\left(0, \mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))\right)\right) \to 0, \end{equation*} and, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, it holds that \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}_n \left(d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation*}
conclusions: d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N\left(0, \mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))\right)\right) \to 0,
\mathbb{P}_n \left(d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0.
nodes.statement_short: Under Condition 1 the standardized estimation error is close in $d_w$ to $N(0,\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)))$, and with $S_n$ standardization to $N(0,\mathrm{corr}(S_n))$.
nodes.label: lemma:equivSn

nodes.name: Pollak's characterization of normality of infinitely divisible laws
nodes.statement: To verify that marginal Lindeberg conditions are sufficient for our theory to go through, we exploit a result due to \cite{pollak1972}, showing that an infinitely-divisible distribution is normal if and only if each of its marginals is normal.
conclusions: an infinitely-divisible distribution is normal if and only if each of its marginals is normal
equivalent_conditions: each of its marginals is normal

nodes.name: Equivalent formulation of the marginal Lindeberg condition
nodes.statement: Using, e.g., \cite{gnedenko} Theorem 3 in Paragraph 21, one obtains that Equation \eqref{eq:linde} in Condition \ref{cond:sum} can be \emph{equivalently} phrased as \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}_n\circ \left( \frac{r_n^{(j)}}{\mathbb{V}^{1/2}_n(r_n^{(j)})} \right) &\Rightarrow N(0, 1) \quad\text{and}\\[7pt] \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{P}_n \left(|g_{i,n}^{(j)} | \geq \varepsilon\mathbb{V}^{1/2}_n(r_n^{(j)}) \right) &\to 0\; \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0. \end{align*} In some applications it might be easier to check these two conditions directly (for every $j$), in particular in case one can use existing results in the literature on misspecified models without model selection as indicated above.
nodes.statement_short: The Lindeberg condition (2.3) is equivalent to marginal asymptotic normality plus uniform asymptotic negligibility.
nodes.label: rem:lindeequiv

nodes.name: Offset $\rho(\mathbb{M})$
nodes.statement: Given $\mathbb{M} = \mathbb{M}_{j,n} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ we abbreviate \begin{equation*} \rho(\mathbb{M}) \quad := \quad \sum_{l = 1}^{j-1} m(\mathbb{M}_{l,n}), \end{equation*} where sums over an empty index set are to be interpreted as $0$.

nodes.name: Coverage with a consistent covariance estimator
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, suppose Condition \ref{cond:sum} holds, and let $\hat{S}_n: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^{k \times k}$ be a sequence of Borel-measurable functions so that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_n) - \mathrm{corr}\left(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)\right)\| + \| \mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n) - I_k \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \end{equation*} converges to $0$, or equivalently, that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_n) - \mathrm{corr}\left(S_n\right)\| + \| \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger} \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n) - I_k \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Define for every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ and every $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ the confidence interval \begin{equation*} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \quad = \quad \hat{\theta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{[\hat{S}_n]_{\rho(\mathbb M) + j }} ~ K_{1-\alpha}\left(\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_n)\right). \end{equation*} Then, $ \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \text{ for all } \mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n \text{ and all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M}) \right) $ converges to $1-\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, for every (measurable) model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$, we have \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5.1 Confidence intervals based on consistent estimators of $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$
assumptions: let $\hat{S}_n: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^{k \times k}$ be a sequence of Borel-measurable functions
conclusions: converges to $1-\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$.

\liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha.
nodes.statement_short: With a covariance estimator consistent in the correlation/diagonal sense, intervals using $K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\hat S_n))$ have asymptotic simultaneous coverage $1-\alpha$ for any selection.

nodes.name: Consistent covariance estimation from predictors of the summands
nodes.statement: Suppose Condition \ref{cond:sum} is satisfied, and let $\hat{g}_{i,n}: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ be Borel measurable for $i = 1, \hdots, n$ and for every $n$. Suppose that for every $j = 1, \hdots, k$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n \left(g_{i,n}^{(j)} - \hat{g}_{i,n}^{(j)} \right)^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n [g_{i,n}^{(j)}]^2} \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0, \end{equation} or equivalently that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n \left(g_{i,n}^{(j)} - \hat{g}_{i,n}^{(j)} \right)^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n \mathbb{V}_n \left( g_{i,n}^{(j)}\right)} \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Then the convergence in \eqref{eq:consest} is satisfied for \begin{equation*} \hat{S}_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n \hat{g}_{i,n}\hat{g}'_{i,n}. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: Suppose Condition \ref{cond:sum} is satisfied, and let $\tilde{g}_{i,n}: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $\hat{g}_{i,n}: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ be Borel measurable for $i = 1, \hdots, n$ and for every $n$. Suppose that for every $j = 1, \hdots, k$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the condition \eqref{eq:negldiff}, or equivalently \eqref{eq:negldiff2}, is satisfied. nodes.name: Consistency when the bias terms are negligible
nodes.statement: Using the simple bound $(g_{i,n}^{(j)} - \tilde{g}_{i,n}^{(j)})^2 \le 2(g_{i,n}^{(j)} - \hat{g}_{i,n}^{(j)})^2 + 2 a_{i,n}^2$, it is easy to verify that if the non-stochastic additive components $a_{i,n}$ are negligible in the previously defined sense, then $\tilde{g}_{i,n}$ satisfies the assumptions of $\hat{g}_{i,n}$ appearing in Proposition \ref{prop:obtest}. As a consequence, the estimator \begin{equation*} \tilde{S}_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n \tilde{g}_{i,n}\tilde{g}'_{i,n} \end{equation*} satisfies \eqref{eq:consest}, and one can construct confidence intervals based on this estimator as discussed in Theorem \ref{thm:fbl}. Note that $\hat{\nu}^2_{j,n} = [\tilde{S}_n]_{j}$.

nodes.name: Upper-bound constant $B_{\alpha}(q,N)$
nodes.statement: The bound we shall discuss is based on the quantity $B_{\alpha}(q,N)$, for $q,N \in \mathbb{N}$, defined as the smallest $t >0$ so that \[ \mathbb{E}_G \left( \min\left(1, N \left[ 1 - F_{Beta,1/2,(q-1)/2} (t^2/G^2) \right] \right) \right) \leq \alpha, \] where $F_{Beta,1/2,(q-1)/2}$ is the cumulative distribution function of the \linebreak Beta($1/2$,$(q-1)/2$) distribution, and where $G^2$ follows a chi-squared distribution with $q$ degrees of freedom.

nodes.label: lem:upper

nodes.name: Observation vector $Y_n$
nodes.statement: The scenarios we discuss in this section are all concerned with the case $\ell=1$ (the case $\ell>1$ is of interest, e.g., in a regression problem with random design where one observes a data matrix $(y_i, x_{i1}, \dots, x_{ip})_{i=1}^n$ which is a realization of a probability distribution ${\mathbb P}_n$ on the sample space ${\mathbb R}^{n\times (p+1)}$), that is, we observe realizations of a random $n$-vector $Y_n=(Y_{1,n}, \dots, Y_{n,n})'$ defined on some probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal A, {\mathbb P})$, whose distribution under ${\mathbb P}$ coincides with ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n$ (we write ${\mathbb E}$ and ${\mathbb V}$ to denote the expectation and variance-covariance operator with respect to ${\mathbb P}$).

nodes.name: Homoskedastic feasible set $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$
nodes.statement: The feasible sets for the true underlying distribution $\mathbb{P}_n$ we can allow for in this setup is denoted as $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}\left(\delta, \tau \right)$, where $\delta > 0$ and $\tau \ge 1$, and is defined as follows: the distribution ${\mathbb P}_n$ of the random $n$-vector $Y_n = (Y_{1,n}, \hdots, Y_{n,n})'$ is an element of $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}\left(\delta, \tau \right)$ if and only if the $n$ coordinates of $Y_n$ are independent, homoskedastic (i.e., the variances of the coordinates are equal to some ${\mathbb V}(Y_{i,n}) = \sigma_n^2 \in (0, \infty)$, for all $i=1,\dots, n$), and \begin{equation*} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}\left(|Y_{i,n} - \mathbb{E}(Y_{i,n})|^{2+\delta}\right)^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}} \leq \tau \sigma_n^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.statement_short: Independent homoskedastic coordinates whose $(2+\delta)$-moments are bounded by $\tau$ times the variance.

nodes.name: Properties of $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$ is empty for $\delta>0$ and $\tau< 1$, because then the inequality in the previous display can never be satisfied. Furthermore, observe that $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$ contains the set of $n$-variate spherical normal distributions with unrestricted mean vector if $$ \mathbf{\Gamma}\left( \frac{3+\delta}{2}\right) \le \left( \tau/2 \right)^{1+\delta/2}\sqrt{\pi}, $$ where $\mathbf{\Gamma}(.)$ denotes the Gamma-function. For such a pair $(\delta,\tau)$ the set $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$ thus contains the Gaussian model considered in \citet{Berk13}. Finally note that there is no restriction on the mean vector $\mu_n = {\mathbb E}(Y_n)\in{\mathbb R}^n$ of elements of $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.statement_short: The set is empty for $\tau<1$, contains spherical Gaussians for suitable $(\delta,\tau)$, and leaves the mean unrestricted.

nodes.name: Design matrix $X_n$
nodes.statement: That is, a situation where one wants to conduct inference on the mean vector $\mu_n$ of the underlying distribution $\mathbb{P}_n$, and it is \emph{assumed} by the practitioner that $\mu_n$ is an element of $\mathrm{span}(X_n)$, the column span of a design matrix $X_n \in {\mathbb R}^{n \times p}$, with $p$ not depending on $n$, or that $\mu_n$ is at least ``well-approximated'' by an element of that linear space; and that the practitioner \textit{knows} (and takes into account in the construction of the confidence sets) that the observations have identical variances (for a situation where the observations are heteroskedastic see Subsection~\ref{sec:hetlinmods}).
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Collection $\mathcal{I}$ of candidate regressor sets
nodes.statement: We assume that we are given a nonempty set $\mathcal{I} = \{M_1, \hdots, M_d\}$ of nonempty subsets of $\{1, 2, \hdots, p\}$, that does not depend on $n$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Submatrix $X_n[M]$
nodes.statement: Given $M \in \mathcal{I}$ we shall denote by $X_n[M]$ the matrix obtained from $X_n$ by striking all columns whose index is not an element of $M$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Linear homoskedastic candidate model
nodes.statement: We then consider for each $j \in \{1, \hdots, d\}$ a linear, homoskedastic candidate model $\mathbb{M}_{j, n}$ with fixed design $X_n[M_j]$, i.e., the distribution of a random vector $z = (z_1, \hdots, z_n)'$ is an element of $\mathbb{M}_{j, n}$ if and only if there exists a $\beta \in {\mathbb R}^{|M_j|}$ so that the random (residual) vector $z - X_n[M_j]\beta$ has independent, homoskedastic coordinates with mean zero.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Rows of the design
nodes.statement: We assume that $X_n$ satisfies the following condition, where we denote the $i$-th row of $X_n$ by $X_{i,n}$:
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Condition on the design (vanishing leverage)
nodes.statement: Eventually $\mathrm{rank}(X_n) = p$, and for every $M\in\mathcal I$, \begin{equation*} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M] \left( X_{n}[M]'X_{n}[M] \right)^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \to 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.statement_short: Eventually full rank, and maximal leverage of every candidate submodel tends to 0.
nodes.label: cond:X

nodes.name: Sufficient conditions for the design condition
nodes.statement: Condition~\ref{cond:X} particularly holds if $\mathrm{rank}(X_n) = p$, eventually, and $\max_{i=1,\dots, n} X_{i,n}(X_n'X_n)^{-1}X_{i,n}' \to 0$. Moreover, it also holds in case $\|X_{i,n}\|$ is bounded and $\lambda_{\min}(\frac{1}{n} X_n'X_n)$ is bounded away from $0$, which is typically the case in sufficiently balanced factorial designs, but Condition~\ref{cond:X} is obviously much more general. For example, it also covers the important cases of polynomial regressors, trigonometric regressors, or mixed polynomial and trigonometric regressors (cf. the discussion in \cite{eicker67}, pp. 64). Finally, we point out that the condition \begin{equation*} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M] \left( X_{n}[M]'X_{n}[M] \right)^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \to 0 \end{equation*} is classical, and is necessary for asymptotic normality of the ordinary-least-squares estimator in the fixed model $\mathbb M$ \citep[see][]{Huber73, Arnold80}.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Projection target $\beta^*_{\mathbb{M},n}$ in linear models
nodes.statement: The model-specific target of inference is then (eventually) defined as follows: Given $\mathbb{M}\in \mathsf{M}_n$ with a corresponding index set $M$, we let \begin{equation} \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^* = \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^*(\mathbb{P}_n) = \left(X_n[M]'X_n[M]\right)^{-1} X_n[M]' \mu_n, \end{equation} i.e., $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*$ is the coefficient vector corresponding to the orthogonal projection of $\mu_n$ onto $\mathrm{span}(X_n[M])$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data

nodes.name: Equation (3.1) [eqn:targethom]
nodes.statement: \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^* = \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^*(\mathbb{P}_n) = \left(X_n[M]'X_n[M]\right)^{-1} X_n[M]' \mu_n,
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.label: eqn:targethom

nodes.name: POSI confidence intervals for homoskedastic linear models
nodes.statement: We shall now describe how asymptotically uniformly valid confidence sets can be constructed post-model-selection for the target defined in Equation \eqref{eqn:targethom} above: Given $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ with index set $M$, we estimate the corresponding target by the model-specific ordinary-least-squares estimator, i.e., by \begin{equation} \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb{M}, n}(y) = \left(X_n[M]'X_n[M]\right)^{-1} X_n[M]'y; \end{equation} let \begin{equation*} \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M}, n}(y) = \frac{1}{n- m(\mathbb{M})} \sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - X_{i,n}[M] \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb{M}, n}(y) )^2, \end{equation*} where $m(\mathbb{M})$ here coincides with $|M|$, the cardinality of $M$, and define for $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ \begin{equation} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M}, n} \left[\left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}\right]_j} K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)), \end{equation} where the block-matrix $\Gamma_n$ is defined via its $s,t$-th block of dimension $|M_s|\times|M_t|$ given by \begin{align*} &{\mathbb E}_n\left[ \left(\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M_s,n} - \beta^*_{\mathbb M_s,n}\right) \left(\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M_t,n} - \beta^*_{\mathbb M_t,n}\right)' \right] \\ &\quad= \sigma_n^2\left( X_n[M_s]' X_n[M_s] \right)^{-1} X_n[M_s]' X_n[M_t] \left( X_n[M_t]' X_n[M_t] \right)^{-1}, \end{align*} for $s, t \in \{1, \hdots, d\}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.statement_short: OLS estimate $\pm$ usual standard error times the POSI constant $K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n))$, with $\Gamma_n$ the joint OLS covariance.

nodes.name: Equation (3.2) [eq:OLS]
nodes.statement: \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb{M}, n}(y) = \left(X_n[M]'X_n[M]\right)^{-1} X_n[M]'y;
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.label: eq:OLS

nodes.name: Equation (3.3) [eq:POSICIlm]
nodes.statement: \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M}, n} \left[\left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}\right]_j} K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)),
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
nodes.label: eq:POSICIlm

nodes.name: Uniform validity of POSI intervals for homoskedastic linear models
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\delta > 0$ and $\tau \ge 1$, suppose Condition~\ref{cond:X} holds, and let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a (measurable) model selection procedure, i.e., a measurable map from the sample space ${\mathbb R}^n$ to $\mathsf{M}_n$. Then \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.1 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to homoskedastic data
assumptions: let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a (measurable) model selection procedure
conclusions: \liminf_{n \to \infty} \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha.
nodes.statement_short: POSI intervals for homoskedastic linear models are asymptotically uniformly valid over $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$ for any selection procedure.
nodes.label: thm:homlinmods

nodes.name: Single-coefficient target $\eta^*_{\mathbb{M},n}$
nodes.statement: Whereas the candidate models in $\mathsf{M}_n$ are still defined as above, the model-specific target vector changes: Now, for every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ the target is the first coordinate of the vector $\beta^*_{\mathbb{M}, n}$ defined in \eqref{eqn:targethom}, which we denote as $\eta^*_{\mathbb{M}, n}$.

nodes.name: Single-coefficient estimator $\hat{\eta}_{\mathbb{M},n}$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, in each model $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ we estimate this target by $\hat{\eta}_{\mathbb{M}, n}$, the first coordinate of the model-specific OLS estimator defined in \eqref{eq:OLS}.

nodes.name: Matrix $\Xi_n$
nodes.statement: Finally, to define our confidence intervals in this case, let $\Xi_n$ denote the $d \times d$-dimensional matrix with $s,t$-th entry given by \begin{equation*} \sigma_n^2\left[ \left( X_n[M_s]' X_n[M_s] \right)^{-1} X_n[M_s]' X_n[M_t] \left( X_n[M_t]' X_n[M_t] \right)^{-1} \right]_{1}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: POSI interval for an individual coefficient
nodes.statement: Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, define for every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ with corresponding index set $M$ the confidence interval \begin{equation*} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}} = \hat{\eta}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M}, n} \left[ (X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{-1} \right]_1} K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Xi_n)). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Individual POSI constant is smaller
nodes.statement: From the definition of $K_{1-\alpha}$, together with the relationship of $\Xi_n$ and $\Gamma_n$, it follows immediately that $$K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Xi_n)) \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)),$$ with equality holding only if $\mathcal{I} = \{\{1\}\}$, i.e., no model selection.
conclusions: $$K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Xi_n)) \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)),$$
with equality holding only if $\mathcal{I} = \{\{1\}\}$

nodes.name: Coverage of individual coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\delta > 0$ and $\tau \ge 1$, suppose Condition~\ref{cond:X} holds, and let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a (measurable) model selection procedure. Suppose every element of $\mathcal{I}$ contains $1$. Then \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\eta^*_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*}
conclusions: \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\eta^*_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n} \right) \geq 1-\alpha.
nodes.label: thm:homlinmodsindi

nodes.name: Consistency of the OLS variance estimator iff the model is first-order correct
nodes.statement: It is well known that the usual variance estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2$ in model $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$ with index set $M\in\mathcal I$ is consistent for the true error variance $\sigma_n^2$, if and only if, the model $\mathbb M$ is asymptotically first order correct. More specifically, the estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2$ is upward biased when $\mathbb M$ is mean-misspecified and the bias is given by $\|(I_n - P_{X_n[M]})\mu_n/\sigma_n\|^2/(n-|M|)$, where $P_{\dots}$ denotes the projection matrix corresponding to the column span of the matrix indicated in the subscript and where $\mu_n = {\mathbb E}(Y_n)$.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
conclusions: is consistent for the true error variance $\sigma_n^2$, if and only if, the model $\mathbb M$ is asymptotically first order correct.
the estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2$ is upward biased when $\mathbb M$ is mean-misspecified
equivalent_conditions: the usual variance estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2$ in model $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$ with index set $M\in\mathcal I$ is consistent for the true error variance $\sigma_n^2$
the model $\mathbb M$ is asymptotically first order correct

nodes.name: Relative consistency of the OLS variance estimator up to the misspecification bias
nodes.statement: Fix $\delta>0$ and $\tau\ge 1$ and suppose that eventually $\mathrm{rank}(X_n)=p$. For any sequence ${\mathbb P}_n \in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$, the variance estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2(y) = (n-|M|)^{-1}y'(I_n-P_{X_n[M]})y$ satisfies \begin{align*} {\mathbb P}_n\left( \left|\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2}{\sigma_n^2} \left(1 + \frac{\|(I_n-P_{X_n[M]})\mu_n/\sigma_n\|^2}{n-|M|}\right)^{-1} - 1\right| > \varepsilon \right) \;\to\;0, \end{align*} for every $\varepsilon>0$ and for every $M\in\mathcal I$.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
conclusions: for every $\varepsilon>0$ and for every $M\in\mathcal I$.
nodes.statement_short: $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathbb M,n}/\sigma_n^2$ is asymptotically $1$ plus the normalized squared misspecification bias.
nodes.label: prop:lmvarest

nodes.name: Consistency of the post-model-selection variance estimator
nodes.statement: In particular, since the index set $\mathcal I$ is finite, not depending on $n$, Proposition~\ref{prop:lmvarest} shows that the post-model-selection estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\mathbb M}_n,n}^2$ is consistent for $\sigma_n^2$ (on a relative scale) along sequences ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$ with the property that \begin{equation} \frac{\|(I_n-P_{X_n[\hat{M}_n]})\mu_n/\sigma_n\|^2}{n-|\hat{M}_n|} \;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\; 0 \end{equation} in ${\mathbb P}_n$-probability, where $\hat{M}_n$ denotes the index set corresponding to $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
assumptions: along sequences ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$ with the property that
conclusions: the post-model-selection estimator $\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\mathbb M}_n,n}^2$ is consistent for $\sigma_n^2$ (on a relative scale)

nodes.name: Equation (3.4) [eq:CondCons]
nodes.statement: \frac{\|(I_n-P_{X_n[\hat{M}_n]})\mu_n/\sigma_n\|^2}{n-|\hat{M}_n|} \;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\; 0
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
nodes.label: eq:CondCons

nodes.name: Nonexistence of a uniformly consistent variance estimator
nodes.statement: Let $\delta > 0$ and $\tau > 1$. There does \emph{not} exist a sequence of measurable functions $(\hat{\sigma}^2_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\hat{\sigma}^2_{n}: \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, \infty)$, so that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{equation} \sup_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \left| \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_n}{\sigma^2_n} - 1 \right| > \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
conclusions: There does \emph{not} exist a sequence of measurable functions $(\hat{\sigma}^2_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
nodes.label: prop:no:consistent:sigma

nodes.name: Equation (3.5) [eqn:conscounter]
nodes.statement: \sup_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \left| \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_n}{\sigma^2_n} - 1 \right| > \varepsilon \right) \to 0.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 The POSI-intervals automatically adapt to misspecification
nodes.label: eqn:conscounter

nodes.name: Heteroskedastic feasible set $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{het})}(\delta,\tau)$
nodes.statement: The feasible sets for $\mathbb{P}_n$ we consider here again depend on two parameters $\delta > 0$ and $\tau \ge 1$ but, compared to the set $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$ defined above, we now drop the requirement of homoskedasticity: the distribution of a random $n$-vector $Y_n = (Y_{1,n}, \hdots, Y_{n,n})'$ is an element of $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{het})} \left(\delta, \tau \right)$ if and only if the $n$ coordinates of $Y_n$ are independent, the variance $\sigma_{i,n}^2 = {\mathbb V}(Y_{i,n}) \in(0,\infty)$ exists for every $i = 1, \hdots, n$, and \begin{equation*} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \left[\mathbb{E}\left(|Y_{i,n} - \mathbb{E}(Y_{i,n})|\right)^{2+\delta}\right]^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}} \leq \tau \min_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \sigma_{i,n}^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to heteroskedastic data

nodes.name: Linear heteroskedastic candidate model
nodes.statement: We start with a set $\mathcal{I} = \{M_1, \hdots, M_d \}$ as in Subsection~\ref{sec:homlinmods}, and we then define for each $j \in \{1, \hdots, d\}$ the linear, heteroskedastic model $\mathbb{M}_{j, n}$ as follows: the distribution of a random vector $z = (z_1, \hdots, z_n)'$ is an element of $\mathbb{M}_{j, n}$ if and only if there exists a $\beta \in {\mathbb R}^{|M_j|}$ so that the random (residual) vector $z - X[M_j]\beta$ has independent coordinates with positive finite variances and mean zero.
nodes.section: 3.2 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to heteroskedastic data

nodes.name: Eicker estimator
nodes.statement: Define for every $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ with corresponding index set $M$ the Eicker-estimator $\tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n}$ as \begin{equation*} \left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1} X_n[M]' \mathrm{diag}\left(\hat{u}^2_{1,\mathbb{M}}, \hdots, \hat{u}^2_{n,\mathbb{M}} \right) X_n[M] \left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}, \end{equation*} where, for $y\in{\mathbb R}^n$, we let $\hat{u}_{\mathbb{M}}(y) = (\hat{u}_{1, \mathbb{M}}(y), \hdots, \hat{u}_{n, \mathbb{M}}(y))' = y - X_n[M] \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb{M}, n}(y)$, and denote the $j-$th diagonal entry ($j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$) of $\tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n}$ by $\hat{\sigma}^2_{j,\mathbb{M}, n}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to heteroskedastic data
nodes.statement_short: Heteroskedasticity-robust sandwich covariance of the OLS estimator built from squared residuals.

nodes.name: POSI intervals for heteroskedastic linear models
nodes.statement: Finally, given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, we define for each $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ with corresponding index set $M$ and for every $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ the confidence sets \begin{equation*} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{hlm}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{j,\mathbb{M}, n}} B_{\alpha}(\min(k, p),k), \end{equation*} with $k = \sum_{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n} m(\mathbb{M})$, and where $B_\alpha$ is defined at the end of Section~\ref{sec:overest}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to heteroskedastic data

nodes.name: Uniform validity for heteroskedastic linear models
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\delta > 0$ and $\tau \ge 1$, suppose Condition~\ref{cond:X} holds, and let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a (measurable) model selection procedure, i.e., a measurable map from the sample space ${\mathbb R}^n$ to $\mathsf{M}_n$. Then \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{het})} \left(\delta, \tau \right) } \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{hlm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Inference post-model-selection when fitting fixed design linear models to heteroskedastic data
assumptions: let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a (measurable) model selection procedure
conclusions: \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{hlm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha.
nodes.statement_short: Eicker-based intervals with the bound $B_\alpha(\min(k,p),k)$ are asymptotically uniformly valid over $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{het})}(\delta,\tau)$.
nodes.label: thm:hetlinmods

nodes.name: Binary feasible set $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$
nodes.statement: The feasible sets $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$ for ${\mathbb P}_n$ we consider here depend on a parameter $\tau \in (0,1/4)$ and are defined as follows: the distribution of a random vector $Y_n = (Y_{1,n}, \hdots, Y_{n,n})'$ is an element of $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$ if and only if the $n$ coordinates of $Y_n$ are independent, each coordinate $Y_{i,n}$ takes on either $0$ or $1$, and ${\mathbb V}(Y_{i,n})\ge \tau$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Response function
nodes.statement: In binary regression the maintained \emph{modeling assumption} is that the probability of a success on the $i$-th observation ($Y_{i,n}=1$), or equivalently its expectation, is given by $h(X_{i,n}\beta)$, for some $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^p$, some response function $h:{\mathbb R}\to (0,1)$ and where $X_{i,n}$ is the $i$-th row of a design matrix $X_n\in{\mathbb R}^{n\times p}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Link function
nodes.statement: Usually, when $h$ is invertible, $h^{-1}$ is called the link function.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Finite set $\mathcal H$ of response functions
nodes.statement: Classical choices are the logit and the probit functions, but we allow also for other choices of response functions $h$, as long as they belong to a finite set $\mathcal H = \{h_1,\dots, h_{d_1}\}$ of potential candidates, that does not depend on $n$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Candidate binary regression model
nodes.statement: Together with the collection $\mathcal I = \{M_1,\dots, M_{d_2}\}\subseteq 2^{\{1,\dots, p\}}\setminus\varnothing$ of candidate regressor subsets, we can define for every $j_1\in\{1,\dots, d_1\}$ and $j_2\in\{1,\dots, d_2\}$ a candidate binary regression model $\mathbb M_{(j_1,j_2),n}$ as follows: the distribution of a random vector $z = (z_1, \hdots, z_n)'$ is an element of $\mathbb M_{(j_1,j_2),n}$ if and only if the $n$ coordinates of $z$ are independent, each coordinate $z_i$ takes on either $0$ or $1$, and there exists a $\beta \in {\mathbb R}^{|M_{j_2}|}$ so that the mean of $z_i$ equals $h_{j_1}(X_{i,n}[M_{j_2}]\beta)$ for $i = 1, \hdots, n$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Design conditions for binary regression
nodes.statement: Let $C>0$ be fixed. Eventually, we have \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $\mathrm{rank}(X_n) = p$; \item $\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M] \left( X_{n}[M]'X_{n}[M] \right)^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \le C/n$, for every $M \in \mathcal{I}$; \item $\lambda_{\max}(X_n'X_n)/\lambda_{\min}(X_n'X_n) \le C$; \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.label: cond:X2

nodes.name: Conditions on the response functions
nodes.statement: The elements $h\in\mathcal H$ have the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $h:{\mathbb R}\to(0,1)$ is a continuous cumulative distribution function; \item The functions $\phi_1(\gamma) := \log(h(\gamma))$ and $\phi_2(\gamma) := \log(1-h(\gamma))$ are strictly concave on ${\mathbb R}$; \item $h$ is twice continuously differentiable and $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ have strictly negative second derivatives on ${\mathbb R}$; \item The derivative $\dot{h}$ of $h$ is strictly positive on ${\mathbb R}$; \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.label: cond:H

nodes.name: Discussion of the binary design condition
nodes.statement: Condition~\ref{cond:X2} is a strengthened version of Condition~\ref{cond:X}. It is still satisfied if $\|X_{i,n}\|$ is bounded and $\lambda_{\min}(\frac{1}{n}X_n'X_n)$ is bounded away from $0$, as is typically the case in factorial designs. Note, however, that Condition~\ref{cond:X2} is invariant under scaling of $X_n$, so that, in particular, it does not require that $\lambda_{\min}(X_n'X_n)\to\infty$, a condition commonly used to prove consistency of the MLE. Furthermore, Condition~\ref{cond:X2}\eqref{cX2:Huber} is implied by $$ X2(ii')\quad\max_{i=1,\dots, n} X_{i,n}(X_n'X_n)^{-1}X_{i,n}' \le C/n. $$
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Discussion of the response-function conditions
nodes.statement: The Conditions~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:cdf} and \ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:Hdot} are rather natural and essential for parameter identification. Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:C2} is also classical and used to ensure continuity of the Hessian of the log-likelihood \citep[cf.][]{Fahrmeir85, Fahrmeir90}. Finally, Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:concave}, which is implied by Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:C2}, ensures strict concavity of the log-likelihood, which, in turn, guarantees uniqueness of pseudo parameters and the MLE (see Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:unifCons} below). It is easy to see that Condition~\ref{cond:H} is satisfied, e.g., for response functions corresponding to the classical logit, probit, log-log and complementary log-log link functions discussed in \citet[][p.108]{McCullagh89}.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Identification of a model with a pair $(h,M)$
nodes.statement: Note that since the design matrix $X_n\in{\mathbb R}^{n\times p}$ is fixed, a candidate model $\mathbb M \in \mathsf{M}_n$ can be identified with a pair $\mathbb M \triangleq (h, M) \in \mathcal H\times \mathcal I$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: (Quasi-)log-likelihood $\ell_{\mathbb M,n}$
nodes.statement: The (quasi-)log-likelihood function for model $\mathbb M \triangleq (h,M)$ can be expressed as \begin{equation*} \ell_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \phi_1(X_{i,n}[M]\beta) + (1-y_i)\phi_2(X_{i,n}[M]\beta)\right], \end{equation*} where $\phi_1(\gamma) = \log h(\gamma)$ and $\phi_2(\gamma) = \log (1-h(\gamma))$, and $y = (y_1,\dots, y_n)'\in\{0,1\}^n$, $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Negative Hessian $H_{\mathbb M,n}$
nodes.statement: Whenever Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:C2} holds, we denote the matrix of negative second derivatives of $\ell_{\mathbb M,n}$ by $$ H_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta) \;=\; -\frac{\partial^2\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta)}{\partial \beta \partial \beta'} \;=\; X_n[M]'D_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta)X_n[M], $$ where $D_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta)$ is a diagonal matrix with $i$-th diagonal entry equal to $$-y_i \ddot{\phi}_1(X_{i,n}[M]\beta) - (1-y_i)\ddot{\phi}_2(X_{i,n}[M]\beta).$$
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Pseudo-true target $\beta^*_{\mathbb M,n}$ in binary regression
nodes.statement: As our target of inference we take the model dependent vector $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^* \in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ that maximizes the expected log-likelihood $\beta\mapsto {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot,\beta)]$ under the true data generating distribution ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Pseudo-target minimizes Kullback-Leibler divergence
nodes.statement: If $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*$ exists, then it is easy to see that it also minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true data generating distribution ${\mathbb P}_n$ and the class of distributions specified by the working model $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
conclusions: it also minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true data generating distribution ${\mathbb P}_n$ and the class of distributions specified by the working model $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of the pseudo-true parameter
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\mathrm{rank}(X_n)=p$ and \ref{cond:H}(\ref{cH:cdf},\ref{cH:concave}) hold. Then, for every $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$ and for every ${\mathbb P}_n\in\bigcup_{\delta>0}\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\delta)$, there exists a unique vector $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^* = \beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$, such that \begin{equation*} \int_{{\mathbb R}^n} \ell_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)) \,d{\mathbb P}_n(y) \;=\; \sup_{\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}} \int_{{\mathbb R}^n} \ell_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta) \,d{\mathbb P}_n(y). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
conclusions: there exists a unique vector $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^* = \beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$, such that
nodes.label: lemma:pseudo

nodes.name: Asymptotic existence and uniform consistency of the quasi-MLE
nodes.statement: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond:X2}(\ref{cX2:rank},\ref{cX2:Huber}) and \ref{cond:H}(\ref{cH:cdf},\ref{cH:concave},\ref{cH:C2}) hold and fix $\tau\in(0,1/4)$. Then, for every $n\in{\mathbb N}$, every $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$ and every ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$, there exists a function $\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}:\{0,1\}^n\to{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$ (depending only on $n$ and $\mathbb M$) and a set $E_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n}\subseteq \{0,1\}^n$, such that \begin{align*} \ell_{\mathbb M,n}\left(y, \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y) + \beta\right) \;<\; \ell_{\mathbb M,n}\left(y, \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y)\right) \quad \forall y\in\ E_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n},\;\forall \beta\neq 0 \end{align*} and $$\inf_{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n}\inf_{{\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)} {\mathbb P}_n(E_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n}) \;\xrightarrow[n\to \infty]{} \; 1.$$ Moreover, for the pseudo parameter $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo}, we have $$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\substack{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n\\{\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)}} {\mathbb P}_n\left( \left\| (X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{1/2}(\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n} - \beta^*_{\mathbb M,n}({\mathbb P}_n))\right\| > \delta\right)\; \to\; 0, $$ as $\delta\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
conclusions: there exists a function $\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}:\{0,1\}^n\to{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$ (depending only on $n$ and $\mathbb M$) and a set $E_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n}\subseteq \{0,1\}^n$
Moreover, for the pseudo parameter $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo}, we have
nodes.statement_short: With probability tending to one uniformly the quasi-MLE exists uniquely, and it is uniformly $\sqrt{n}$-type consistent for the pseudo-true parameter.
nodes.label: lemma:unifCons

nodes.name: Sandwich variance estimator for binary regression
nodes.statement: For $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$, $\mathbb M \triangleq (h,M)$, define \noeqref{eq:tildeSlogistic} \begin{align} \tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n} = \hat{H}_{\mathbb M,n}^{-1}X_n[M]' \mathrm{diag}\left(\hat{u}^2_{1,\mathbb{M}}, \hdots, \hat{u}^2_{n,\mathbb{M}} \right) X_n[M] \hat{H}_{\mathbb M,n}^{-1}, \end{align} where $\hat{H}_{\mathbb M,n}(y) = H_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y))$, $$ \hat{u}_{i,\mathbb{M}}(y) = \frac{\dot{h}(\hat{\gamma}_{i,n,M}(y))}{h(\hat{\gamma}_{i,n,M}(y))(1-h(\hat{\gamma}_{i,n,M}(y)))}\left(y_i - h(\hat{\gamma}_{i,n,M}(y)) \right) $$ and $\hat{\gamma}_{i,n,M}(y) = X_{i,n}[M]\hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y)$, and denote the $j-$th diagonal entry ($j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$) of $\tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n}$ by \begin{equation} \hat{\sigma}^2_{j,\mathbb{M}, n}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.statement_short: Fahrmeir-type sandwich estimator $\hat H^{-1}X'\mathrm{diag}(\hat u^2)X\hat H^{-1}$ with its diagonal entries $\hat\sigma^2_{j,\mathbb M,n}$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.6) [eq:tildeSlogistic]
nodes.statement: \tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n} = \hat{H}_{\mathbb M,n}^{-1}X_n[M]' \mathrm{diag}\left(\hat{u}^2_{1,\mathbb{M}}, \hdots, \hat{u}^2_{n,\mathbb{M}} \right) X_n[M] \hat{H}_{\mathbb M,n}^{-1},
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.label: eq:tildeSlogistic

nodes.name: Equation (3.7) [eq:Sbinary]
nodes.statement: \hat{\sigma}^2_{j,\mathbb{M}, n}.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.label: eq:Sbinary

nodes.name: POSI intervals for binary regression
nodes.statement: Finally, given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, we define for each $\mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n$ and for every $j = 1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})$ the confidence sets \begin{equation*} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{bin}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \pm \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{j,\mathbb{M}, n}} B_{\alpha}(\min(k, n),k), \end{equation*} with $k = \sum_{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n} m(\mathbb{M})$, and where $B_\alpha$ is as defined at the end of Section~\ref{sec:overest}.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: Uniform validity for binary regression
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and $\tau \in(0,1/4)$, suppose Conditions~\ref{cond:X2} and \ref{cond:H} hold, and let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a model selection procedure, i.e., a map from the sample space $\{0,1\}^n$ to $\mathsf{M}_n$. Then \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \inf_{\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})} \left(\tau \right) } \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{bin}} \;\forall j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
assumptions: let $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ be a model selection procedure
conclusions: \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{* (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{bin}} \;\forall j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich-based intervals with $B_\alpha(\min(k,n),k)$ are asymptotically uniformly valid over $\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$, also when the link is selected.
nodes.label: thm:binary

nodes.name: Smaller constant for the canonical link
nodes.statement: It is important to note that if one decides a priori to use only the canonical link function, which, in the present case of binary regression, corresponds to the logistic response function $h^{(c)}(\gamma) := e^\gamma/(1+e^\gamma)$, then Theorem~\ref{thm:binary} holds with the POSI-constant $B_\alpha(\min(k,n),k)$ decreased to $B_\alpha(\min(k,p),k)$. See Corollary~\ref{corr:binaryCanoncial} in Section~\ref{sec:binaryCanonical} of the supplement.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data
nodes.label: rem:canonical:response:function

nodes.name: Extension to M- and Z-estimation
nodes.statement: We point out that similar principles used to derive Theorem~\ref{thm:binary} can also be employed to treat other quasi-maximum likelihood or general M-, and Z-estimation problems \citep[see, e.g.,][for a more general treatment of generalized linear models]{Fahrmeir90}. The general theory of M- and Z-estimation as presented, e.g., in \citet[][Sections~3.2 and 3.3]{Vaart96}, usually also leads to expansions of the form required in Conditon~\ref{cond:sum} \citep[cf.][Theorem~3.2.16 and Theorem~3.3.1]{Vaart96}. These results are stated in a pointwise fashion but can be made uniform over large classes of data generating processes by using ideas from Section~2.8 of the same reference. However, in more specific examples, such as the present binary regression setting, conditions can be directly imposed on the design and the link functions and can be optimized for this setup.
nodes.section: 3.3 Inference post-model-selection when fitting binary regression models to binary data

nodes.name: significance hunting
nodes.statement: For given $X_n$ and $Y_n$, we first sort all the possible candidate models $\mathbb{M}\in\mathsf M_n$ according to their penalized log-likelihood, with additive penalty term equal to $\lambda |M|$, where $\mathbb{M}$ has index set $M$. Then, for the $n_{best}$ models with largest penalized log-likelihood, we compute all the possible test statistics of the form \[ \frac{ \left| \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M},n} \right| }{ \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M},n} \left[\left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}\right]_j} }, \] with $j =1,...,|M|$. We then return the pair $\hat{\mathbb{M}},\hat{j}$ with largest test statistics.
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure
nodes.statement_short: Rank models by penalized log-likelihood, then among the $n_{best}$ best pick the (model, coefficient) with the largest $t$-statistic.
output: the pair $\hat{\mathbb{M}},\hat{j}$ with largest test statistics
also_stated_at: We first sort all the possible candidate models $\mathbb{M}\in\mathsf M_n$ according to their penalized log-likelihood and then select the model $\mathbb M$ and index $j$ that maximize the test statistics \[ \frac{ \left| \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M},n} \right| }{ \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M},n} \left[\left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}\right]_j} }, \] among the $n_{best}$ models with largest penalized log-likelihood.

nodes.name: Sort models
nodes.statement: For given $X_n$ and $Y_n$, we first sort all the possible candidate models $\mathbb{M}\in\mathsf M_n$ according to their penalized log-likelihood, with additive penalty term equal to $\lambda |M|$, where $\mathbb{M}$ has index set $M$.
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure
nodes.statement_short: Sort candidate models by penalized log-likelihood (penalty $\lambda|M|$).

nodes.name: Compute test statistics
nodes.statement: Then, for the $n_{best}$ models with largest penalized log-likelihood, we compute all the possible test statistics of the form \[ \frac{ \left| \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\mathbb{M},n} \right| }{ \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathbb{M},n} \left[\left( X_n[M]'X_n[M] \right)^{-1}\right]_j} }, \] with $j =1,...,|M|$.
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure
nodes.statement_short: Compute all $t$-type statistics in the $n_{best}$ best models.

nodes.name: Return most significant pair
nodes.statement: We then return the pair $\hat{\mathbb{M}},\hat{j}$ with largest test statistics.
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure

nodes.name: Significance hunting attains exact asymptotic coverage at $\beta=0$
nodes.statement: We also observe that, when $n_{best} = 2^p - 1$ , the ``significance hunting'' procedure corresponds to the SPAR procedure in \cite{Berk13}, and yields an asymptotic coverage exactly equal to $1-\alpha$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:homlinmods}, if $\beta$ is the zero vector, so that all candidate models are first order correct.
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure
conclusions: the ``significance hunting'' procedure corresponds to the SPAR procedure in \cite{Berk13}
yields an asymptotic coverage exactly equal to $1-\alpha$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:homlinmods}

nodes.name: Justification of exact coverage for significance hunting
nodes.statement: [This can be deduced from Proposition~\ref{prop:lmvarest} and Theorem~\ref{thm:fbl}, where Condition~\ref{cond:sum} is verified, e.g., in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:homlinmods}.]
nodes.section: A.1.2 The case of a significance hunting procedure
nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 3.4 and Theorem 2.4, with Condition 1 verified as in the proof of Theorem 3.2.

nodes.name: Naive confidence interval for binary regression
nodes.statement: Finally, we consider the ``naive'' confidence interval defined by \begin{equation} \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{naive}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \pm q_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{ (\bar{S}_{\hat{\mathbb M}_n,n})_{jj} }, \end{equation} where $q_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the $1-\alpha/2$ quantile of the standard Gaussian distribution and where $\bar{S}_{\mathbb M,n}$ is as $\tilde{S}_{\mathbb M,n}$ in \eqref{eq:tildeSlogistic} but with $\hat{u}^2_{i,\mathbb M}$ replaced by $(h^{(c)}(\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbb M,i})(1-h^{(c)}(\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbb M,i})))$ with $\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbb M,i} = X_{i,n} \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}$.
nodes.section: A.2.1 Comparison with the confidence intervals of \cite{taylor17post} and with the naive procedure

nodes.statement: \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{naive}} = \hat{\beta}^{(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \pm q_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{ (\bar{S}_{\hat{\mathbb M}_n,n})_{jj} },

nodes.name: Triangular array $z_{i,n}$
nodes.statement: In this section, for every $n \in {\mathbb N}$ and for some $k \in {\mathbb N}$, not depending on $n$, let $z_{1,n}, \hdots, z_{n,n}$ be independent $k$-variate random vectors defined on a probability space $(\Omega_n, \mathcal{A}_n, \mathbb{P}_n)$.

nodes.name: Row sums $r_n$ and outer-product sums $S_n$ of the array
nodes.statement: Denote \begin{equation} r_n \quad = \quad (r^{(1)}_n, \hdots, r^{(k)}_n)' \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n (z^{(1)}_{i,n}, \hdots, z^{(k)}_{i,n})', \end{equation} and let \begin{equation} S_n \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n z_{i,n} z_{i,n}'. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (B.1)
nodes.statement: r_n \quad = \quad (r^{(1)}_n, \hdots, r^{(k)}_n)' \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n (z^{(1)}_{i,n}, \hdots, z^{(k)}_{i,n})',

nodes.name: Equation (B.2)
nodes.statement: S_n \quad = \quad \sum_{i = 1}^n z_{i,n} z_{i,n}'.

nodes.name: Condition 2 (standardized array)
nodes.statement: For every $n \in {\mathbb N}$, every $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ and every $i \in \{1, \hdots, n\}$ \begin{equation} {\mathbb E}_n(z^{(j)}_{i,n}) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n) = 1. \end{equation} Furthermore, for every $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \circ r^{(j)}_n \quad \Rightarrow \quad N(0,1), \end{equation} and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{equation} \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \mathbb{P}_n\left(|z^{(j)}_{i,n}|\geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation}
nodes.label: cond:zmom

nodes.name: Equation (B.3) [EQ:mom]
nodes.statement: {\mathbb E}_n(z^{(j)}_{i,n}) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n) = 1.
nodes.label: EQ:mom

nodes.name: Equation (B.4) [EQ:conv]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \circ r^{(j)}_n \quad \Rightarrow \quad N(0,1),
nodes.label: EQ:conv

nodes.name: Equation (B.5) [EQ:neg]
nodes.statement: \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \mathbb{P}_n\left(|z^{(j)}_{i,n}|\geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0.
nodes.label: EQ:neg

nodes.name: Multivariate CLT from marginal conditions and consistency of $S_n$
nodes.statement: Suppose Condition~\ref{cond:zmom} holds. Then \begin{equation} d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, \mathbb{V}_n(r_n)) \big) \to 0. \end{equation} Furthermore, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\big \|S_n -\mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \big \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0, \end{equation} and hence that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, S_n) \big) \geq \varepsilon\right) \to 0. \end{equation}
conclusions: d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, \mathbb{V}_n(r_n)) \big) \to 0.
\mathbb{P}_n \left(\big \|S_n -\mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \big \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0,
\mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, S_n) \big) \geq \varepsilon\right) \to 0.
nodes.label: lemma:zmom

nodes.name: Equation (B.6)
nodes.statement: d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, \mathbb{V}_n(r_n)) \big) \to 0.

nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \left(\big \|S_n -\mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \big \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0,
nodes.label: eqn:empvar

nodes.name: Equation (B.8) [eqn:empclt]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w \big( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n, N(0, S_n) \big) \geq \varepsilon\right) \to 0.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.1
nodes.statement: For the first claim, let $n'$ be an arbitrary subsequence. From Equation \eqref{EQ:mom} we see that $\mathbb{E}_n(r_n) = 0$ and that $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$ is norm-bounded and, hence, that $\mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n$ is tight. Therefore, there exists a subsequence $n''$ of $n'$ along which $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$ converges to $\Sigma$, say, and along which $\mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n$ converges weakly. We now need to show that $d_w(\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''}, N(0, \Sigma)) \rightarrow 0$, which then proves the statement in view of the triangle inequality, continuity of $\Gamma \mapsto N(0, \Gamma)$ w.r.t. $d_w$, and the fact that $n'$ was arbitrary. That the weak limit of $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''}$ must be normal follows from Equations \eqref{EQ:conv} and \eqref{EQ:neg}, applying Corollary 2 in \cite{pollak1972}. The mean vector of the limiting distribution of $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''}$ is $0$ from \eqref{EQ:conv}. It remains to verify that the covariance matrix of the limiting distribution is $\Sigma$. From Equations \eqref{EQ:mom} and \eqref{EQ:conv} and, e.g., Theorem 5.4 in \cite{bill2} it follows that $[r_{n}^{(j)}]^2$ is uniformly integrable for $j = 1, \hdots, k$. The inequality $ab \leq \frac{1}{2}(a^2 + b^2)$, together with the fact that the sum of two uniformly integrable sequences is uniformly integrable, then shows uniform integrability of $r_n^{(s)}r_n^{(t)}$, and hence (e.g., again Theorem 5.4 in \cite{bill2} together with weak convergence of $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''}$ and the continuous mapping theorem) that the covariance matrix of the limiting distribution of $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''}$ coincides with $\Sigma$. To prove the second claim, we start with the observation that it suffices to verify that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $\gamma \in {\mathbb R}^k$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left(|\gamma'\left( S_n - \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right) \gamma | \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} To see this, it suffices to first take $\gamma$ equal to the elements of the standard basis in ${\mathbb R}^k$ in order to show that the diagonal entries converge to zero. Then, taking $\gamma$ equal to $(1,1,0,\dots, 0)'$, $(0,1,1,0,\dots, 0)'$, etc., and using symmetry shows that also the entries above and below the main diagonal converge. Continuing this process with vectors containing exactly three, four, five, etc., consecutive ones, establishes the claim. Next, to verify the statement in the previous display, let $\gamma \in {\mathbb R}^k$, $\varepsilon > 0$, and let $n'$ be an arbitrary subsequence. Choose $n''$ a subsequence of $n'$ along which $\mathbb{P}_n \circ r_n \Rightarrow N(0, \Sigma)$ - such a subsequence exists because of the already established part of the lemma. We also already know from the uniform integrability argument above, that then $\mathbb{V}_{n''}(r_{n''}) \rightarrow \Sigma$, and hence that $\sigma_{n''}^2 := \gamma' \mathbb{V}_{n''}(r_{n''}) \gamma \rightarrow \gamma' \Sigma \gamma =: \sigma^2$. Now, if $\sigma^2 = 0$, then eventually $\sigma_{n''}^2 < \varepsilon/2$, and by Markov's inequality \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_{n''} \left(\big|\gamma'\left(S_{n''}-\mathbb{V}_{n''}(r_{n''}) \right)\gamma \big| \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq \mathbb{P}_{n''} \left(\gamma' S_{n''} \gamma \geq \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \right) \leq \frac{2 \sigma_{n''}^2} { \varepsilon} \to 0. \end{equation} Suppose next that $\sigma^2 > 0$. Then, we can assume without loss of generality that $0 <\delta_1 \le \sigma_{n''}^2 \leq \delta$ for some $\delta,\delta_1 \in {\mathbb R}$, and it remains to verify that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_{n''} \left( \left|\frac{\gamma' S_{n''} \gamma}{\sigma_{n''}^2 } - 1 \right| \geq \frac{\varepsilon}{\delta} \right) \to 0. \end{equation} To that end, define \begin{equation} \xi_{i,n''} \quad = \quad \frac{\gamma' z_{i, n''}}{\sigma_{n''}} \end{equation} where $\sigma_{n''}$ denotes the positive square root of $\sigma_{n''}^2$, and note that by Equation~\eqref{EQ:mom} we have $\mathbb{E}_{n''} (\xi_{i,n''} ) = 0$, that by construction $\sigma_{n''}^{-2} \gamma' S_{n''} \gamma = \sum_{i = 1}^{n''} \xi_{i,n''}^2$, and that $\mathbb{V}_{n''}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n''} \xi_{i,n''}) = 1$. Note also that it follows from Equation~\eqref{EQ:neg} that for every $\bar{\delta} > 0$ we have \begin{equation} \max_{1 \leq i \leq n''} \mathbb{P}_{n''} \left(|\xi_{i, n''}| \geq \bar{\delta} \right) \to 0 \text{ as } n'' \rightarrow \infty. \end{equation} Furthermore, since $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ r_{n''} \Rightarrow N(0, \Sigma)$, we see that $\sum_{i = 1}^{n''} \xi_{i,n''}$ is asymptotically normal with mean $0$ and variance $1$. But then Equation~\eqref{eq:remains} follows from Raikov's theorem (\cite{gnedenko}, p. 143, Theorem 4). Since $n'$ was arbitrary, this proves the second statement. The statement in Equation \eqref{eqn:empclt} is an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the first two statements.
nodes.statement_short: Subsequence/tightness argument with Pollak's corollary for normal limits; Raikov's theorem for $S_n$. Uniform integrability identifies the limiting covariance.

nodes.name: Condition 3 (non-standardized array)
nodes.statement: For every $n \in {\mathbb N}$, every $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ and every $i \in \{1, \hdots, n\}$ we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_n(z^{(j)}_{i,n}) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad 0 < \mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n) < \infty. \end{equation} Furthermore, setting $r^{(j)}_{n,*} = \frac{r^{(j)}_{n}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n)}}$ and $z^{(j)}_{i, n, *} = \frac{z^{(j)}_{i, n}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n)}}$, for every $j \in \{1, \hdots, k\}$ we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \circ r^{(j)}_{n,*} \Rightarrow N(0,1), \end{equation} and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{equation} \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \mathbb{P}_n\left(|z^{(j)}_{i,n, *}|\geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty. \end{equation}
nodes.label: cond:zmomstd

nodes.name: Equation (B.14) [EQ:momsts]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}_n(z^{(j)}_{i,n}) = 0 \quad \text{ and } \quad 0 < \mathbb{V}_n(r^{(j)}_n) < \infty.

nodes.name: Equation (B.15) [EQ:convstd]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \circ r^{(j)}_{n,*} \Rightarrow N(0,1),

nodes.statement: \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \mathbb{P}_n\left(|z^{(j)}_{i,n, *}|\geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty.

nodes.name: Consistency of diagonal and correlation of $S_n$
nodes.statement: Suppose Condition~\ref{cond:zmomstd} holds. Then, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Furthermore, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\hat{r}_{n,*} = \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} ~ r_n$ satisfies \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left(d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \hat{r}_{n,*} , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \rightarrow 0. \end{equation}
conclusions: \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0
\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0.
