nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.2
nodes.statement: For the statements in Equations \eqref{EQ:diags} and \eqref{EQ:corrs} we first note that the triangular array $z_{i,n,*}^{(j)}$, and the corresponding quantities $r_{n, *}$ and $r_{n,*}^{(j)}$, satisfy Condition \ref{cond:zmom}. Hence, Lemma \ref{lemma:zmom} is applicable, and shows, in particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and with the abbreviation $S_{n,*} = \sum_{i = 1}^n z_{i,n,*} z_{i,n,*}'$, that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\| S_{n,*} -\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n, *}) \| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \quad \text{ as } n \rightarrow \infty . \end{equation} Noting that the diagonal entries of $\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n, *})$ are all equal to $1$ (in fact $\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n, *})$ $=$ $\mathrm{corr} (\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n}))$) and that $\mathrm{diag} \left(S_{n,*}\right) = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n)$ holds, establishes the claimed convergence in \eqref{EQ:diags}. But this together with the preceding display then establishes the convergence in \eqref{EQ:corrs}, because, using the abbreviation $A_n = \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2}\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{1/2}$, we have $A_n \to I_k$ in $\mathbb{P}_n$-probability and \begin{align*} \mathrm{corr}(S_n) - \mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)) &= \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} S_n \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} - \mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,*})\\ &= A_n (S_{n,*} - \mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,*}) ) A_n' \\ &\quad+ A_n \mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,*}) A_n' - \mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,*}), \end{align*} which converges to zero in $\mathbb{P}_n$-probability. The last part is an application of the statements already established, together with \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w\left( \mathbb{P}_n \circ r_{n, *}, N(0, S_{n,*}) \right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0, \end{equation} which we obtain (as above) from Lemma \ref{lemma:zmom}.
nodes.statement_short: Standardize the array, apply Lemma B.1, and transfer convergence to diagonal and correlation matrices.

nodes.name: Continuity of the POSI constant
nodes.statement: For every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ the map $\Gamma \mapsto K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$ is continuous on the subset of $k \times k$-dimensional covariance matrices of ${\mathbb R}^{k \times k}$.
conclusions: the map $\Gamma \mapsto K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$ is continuous on the subset of $k \times k$-dimensional covariance matrices of ${\mathbb R}^{k \times k}$.
nodes.label: lemma:POSIcont

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.3
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma_n$ be a sequence of covariance matrices converging to $\Gamma$. By definition, $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n)$ is the $1-\alpha$-quantile of the distribution of $\|Z_n\|_{\infty}$, where $Z_n$ is a Gaussian random vector with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\Gamma_n$. By the continuous mapping theorem, $\|Z_n\|_{\infty}$ converges weakly to $\|Z\|_{\infty}$, where $Z$ is a Gaussian random vector with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\Gamma$. In case $\Gamma \neq 0$ it is easy to see that the distribution function of $\|Z\|_{\infty}$ is everywhere continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and the result then follows, because weak convergence of distribution functions is equivalent to weak convergence of the corresponding quantile functions. Consider now the case where $\Gamma = 0$. Fix $0 < \varepsilon < 1$. Let $z$ be a random variable taking values in $[0, \infty)$, with continuous and strictly increasing (on $[0,\infty)$) distribution function and $1-\alpha$-quantile equal to $\varepsilon$. Clearly, $\|Z_n\|_{\infty} + z$ converges weakly to $z$. Hence $K_n$, say, the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\|Z_n\|_{\infty} + z$ converges to $\varepsilon$. From $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \leq K_n$ it then follows that \begin{equation*} 0 \quad \leq \quad \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \quad \leq \quad \varepsilon. \end{equation*} Therefore, $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \to 0 = K_{1-\alpha}(0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous mapping plus continuity of quantiles; the degenerate case $\Gamma=0$ via an auxiliary smoothing variable.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma_n$ be a sequence of covariance matrices converging to $\Gamma$. By definition, $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n)$ is the $1-\alpha$-quantile of the distribution of $\|Z_n\|_{\infty}$, where $Z_n$ is a Gaussian random vector with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\Gamma_n$. By the continuous mapping theorem, $\|Z_n\|_{\infty}$ converges weakly to $\|Z\|_{\infty}$, where $Z$ is a Gaussian random vector with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\Gamma$.

nodes.statement_short: Nondegenerate case: continuous strictly increasing cdf gives quantile convergence.

nodes.name: Case $\Gamma=0$
nodes.statement: Consider now the case where $\Gamma = 0$. Fix $0 < \varepsilon < 1$. Let $z$ be a random variable taking values in $[0, \infty)$, with continuous and strictly increasing (on $[0,\infty)$) distribution function and $1-\alpha$-quantile equal to $\varepsilon$. Clearly, $\|Z_n\|_{\infty} + z$ converges weakly to $z$. Hence $K_n$, say, the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\|Z_n\|_{\infty} + z$ converges to $\varepsilon$. From $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \leq K_n$ it then follows that \begin{equation*} 0 \quad \leq \quad \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \quad \leq \quad \varepsilon. \end{equation*} Therefore, $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma_n) \to 0 = K_{1-\alpha}(0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Degenerate case: compare with $\|Z_n\|_\infty+z$ to squeeze the quantile to $0$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary convergence results for sums of squares
nodes.statement: For $n \in {\mathbb N}$, for every $i = 1, \hdots, n$, and for $j = 1, 2$, let $a_{i,n}(j)$ and $b_{i,n}(j)$ be random variables on a probability space $(\Omega_n, \mathcal{A}_n, \mathbb{P}_n)$. Furthermore, let $a_{i,n}=a_{i,n}(1)$ and $b_{i,n}=b_{i,n}(1)$. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\mathbb{P}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n} = 0) \to 0$ holds, and if $\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n} } = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$, then \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \bigg| \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n} }{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} - 1 \bigg| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \quad \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0. \end{equation} \item If $\mathbb{P}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(j) = 0) \to 0$ and $\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n}(j) - b_{i,n}(j))^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(j) } = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$ holds for $j = 1, 2$, then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_n \bigg( \bigg | \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}(1) a_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \\[7pt] & \hspace{3cm} - \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1) b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}^2(1)} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n}(2)}} \bigg | \geq \varepsilon \bigg) \to 0. \end{align} \item Suppose that $\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}) > 0$ holds eventually. Assume that for every $n$ the random variables $a_{i,n}$ for $i = 1, \hdots, n$ have mean $0$ and are uncorrelated, and that it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n\left(\bigg|\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1\bigg| > \varepsilon\right) \to 0 \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0, \end{equation} that \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})} {\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \to 0, \end{equation} and that $\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n} } = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$. Then for every array of real numbers $c_{i,n}$ we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \leq 1 - \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \quad \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0. \end{equation} \end{enumerate}
assumptions: If $\mathbb{P}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n} = 0) \to 0$ holds, and if $\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n} } = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$
conclusions: Then for every array of real numbers $c_{i,n}$ we have
nodes.statement_short: Three lemmas: relative closeness of sums of squares, of empirical correlations, and asymptotic overestimation when adding deterministic shifts.
nodes.label: lemma:auxi

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.4
nodes.statement: For the first part note that the quotient under consideration is well defined with probability converging to one, that \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n} }{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} - 1 = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) + 2 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n} [b_{i,n} - a_{i,n}]}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}, \end{equation} and that by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \begin{equation} \bigg| \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n} [b_{i,n} - a_{i,n}]}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} \bigg| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1). \end{equation} For the second part note that the quotients are well defined with probability converging to 1 (by applying Part 1), and write \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}(1) a_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} - \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1) b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}^2(1)} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n}(2)}} \end{equation} as the sum of \begin{align} A_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n \big(a_{i,n}(1) - b_{i,n}(1)\big)\big(a_{i,n}(2) - b_{i,n}(2)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \\[7pt] B_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(2) \big(a_{i,n}(1) - b_{i,n}(1)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \\[7pt] C_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1)\big(a_{i,n}(2) - b_{i,n}(2)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \end{align} and \begin{align} D_n :&= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1)b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} - \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1) b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}^2(1)} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n}(2)}}. \end{align} Using Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the assumptions, and the first part of the lemma, we now see that $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$ are $o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$. For the third part we note that (eventually) \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 \quad = \quad F_n + G_n + H_n, \end{equation} where \begin{align} F_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \\[7pt] G_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})}+ o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \\[7pt] H_n \quad &:= \quad 2 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n(b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})(a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \end{align} where the second equality for $F_n$ follows from the last assumption appearing in Part 3 together with \eqref{eqn:consia}, and the second equality for $G_n$ follows from \eqref{eqn:consia}. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the last assumption appearing in Part 3 \begin{equation} |H_n| \leq o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \sqrt{G_n + 1}. \end{equation} Now, define \begin{equation} \kappa_n \quad = \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \end{equation} and note that, since by assumption $\mathbb{E}_n(a_{i,n}) = 0$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_n(\kappa_n) = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} =: d_n \geq 0, \end{equation} and it holds, using uncorrelatedness of $a_{i,n}$ for $i = 1, \hdots, n$, that \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n(\kappa_n) = 4 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2 \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}^2_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \leq 4 \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} ~ d_n. \end{equation} We need to verify that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( F_n + G_n + H_n \leq - \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} We argue by contradiction: Suppose there exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ so that the convergence in the previous display does not hold. Then, by compactness of the Cartesian product of the extended real line with the unit interval, there exists a subsequence $n'$ along which $d_n$ converges to a $c \in [0, \infty]$ and along which the probability in the previous display converges to a $\gamma \in (0, 1] $. Suppose first that $0 \leq c < \infty$. Then, from Equation \eqref{eqn:kappavb} and Assumption \eqref{eqn:maxto0}, we see that $\kappa_{n'}$, and hence $G_{n'}$, converges to $c$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and, by Equation \eqref{eqn:Hnbound}, that $H_{n'}$ converges to $0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, showing that $F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'}$ converges to $c \geq 0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and hence that the sequence in the previous display converges along $n'$ to $0<\gamma$, a contradiction. Assume next that $c = \infty$, and assume then, without loss of generality, that $d_{n'} > 0$ holds. We show that $(F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'})/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, which then again contradicts $\gamma \in (0, 1]$. Note that it suffices to verify that $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability. But this follows, because the expectation of $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ is $1$, and because, by relation~\eqref{eqn:kappavb}, its variance is bounded from above by \begin{equation} 4 d_{n'}^{-1} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n'} \mathbb{V}_{n'}(a_{i,n'})}{ \mathbb{V}_{n'}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n'} a_{i,n'})} \to 0, \end{equation} where we used $d_{n'} \to \infty$ and Assumption~\eqref{eqn:maxto0} to obtain the limit.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz decompositions for parts 1-2; part 3 by contradiction along subsequences. The key step bounds the variance of $\kappa_n$ by the Feller ratio.

nodes.name: Part 1
nodes.statement: For the first part note that the quotient under consideration is well defined with probability converging to one, that \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n} }{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} - 1 = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) + 2 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n} [b_{i,n} - a_{i,n}]}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}, \end{equation} and that by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \begin{equation} \bigg| \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n} [b_{i,n} - a_{i,n}]}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} \bigg| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Part 1 via expansion and Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.statement: \bigg| \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n} [b_{i,n} - a_{i,n}]}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}} \bigg| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} - b_{i,n})^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}}} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1).

nodes.name: Part 2
nodes.statement: For the second part note that the quotients are well defined with probability converging to 1 (by applying Part 1), and write \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}(1) a_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} - \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1) b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}^2(1)} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n}(2)}} \end{equation} as the sum of \begin{align} A_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n \big(a_{i,n}(1) - b_{i,n}(1)\big)\big(a_{i,n}(2) - b_{i,n}(2)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \\[7pt] B_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(2) \big(a_{i,n}(1) - b_{i,n}(1)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \\[7pt] C_n &:= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1)\big(a_{i,n}(2) - b_{i,n}(2)\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} \end{align} and \begin{align} D_n :&= \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1)b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n}^2(1) } \sqrt{ \sum_{i = 1}^n a^2_{i,n}(2)}} - \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}(1) b_{i,n}(2)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,n}^2(1)} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^n b^2_{i,n}(2)}}. \end{align} Using Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the assumptions, and the first part of the lemma, we now see that $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$ are $o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Part 2: decompose the difference of correlations into $A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n$, each $o_P(1)$.

nodes.name: Part 3 decomposition
nodes.statement: For the third part we note that (eventually) \begin{equation} \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 \quad = \quad F_n + G_n + H_n, \end{equation} where \begin{align} F_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \\[7pt] G_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})}+ o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \\[7pt] H_n \quad &:= \quad 2 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n(b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})(a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \end{align} where the second equality for $F_n$ follows from the last assumption appearing in Part 3 together with \eqref{eqn:consia}, and the second equality for $G_n$ follows from \eqref{eqn:consia}.
nodes.statement_short: Part 3: decompose the normalized sum into $F_n+G_n+H_n$.

nodes.statement: \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 \quad = \quad F_n + G_n + H_n,

nodes.statement: F_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} = o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)

nodes.statement: G_n \quad &:= \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})^2}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} - 1 = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})}+ o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1)
nodes.label: eqn:Gn

nodes.statement: H_n \quad &:= \quad 2 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n(b_{i,n} - a_{i,n})(a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})}

nodes.name: Bound on $H_n$
nodes.statement: By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the last assumption appearing in Part 3 \begin{equation} |H_n| \leq o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \sqrt{G_n + 1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|H_n|$ by $o_P(1)\sqrt{G_n+1}$.

nodes.statement: |H_n| \leq o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1) \sqrt{G_n + 1}.
nodes.label: eqn:Hnbound

nodes.name: Define $\kappa_n$
nodes.statement: Now, define \begin{equation} \kappa_n \quad = \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \end{equation} and note that, since by assumption $\mathbb{E}_n(a_{i,n}) = 0$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_n(\kappa_n) = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} =: d_n \geq 0, \end{equation} and it holds, using uncorrelatedness of $a_{i,n}$ for $i = 1, \hdots, n$, that \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n(\kappa_n) = 4 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2 \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}^2_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \leq 4 \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} ~ d_n. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\kappa_n$; compute its mean $d_n$ and bound its variance.

nodes.statement: \kappa_n \quad = \quad \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}(2a_{i,n} + c_{i,n})}{ \mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})}

nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}_n(\kappa_n) = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} =: d_n \geq 0,

nodes.name: Equation (B.42) [eqn:kappavb]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{V}_n(\kappa_n) = 4 \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n c_{i,n}^2 \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}^2_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} \leq 4 \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{V}_n(a_{i,n})}{\mathbb{V}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_{i,n})} ~ d_n.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to verify that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( F_n + G_n + H_n \leq - \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Remains to show $P(F_n+G_n+H_n\le-\varepsilon)\to0$.

nodes.name: Equation (B.43)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}_n \left( F_n + G_n + H_n \leq - \varepsilon \right) \to 0.

nodes.name: Contradiction argument
nodes.statement: We argue by contradiction: Suppose there exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ so that the convergence in the previous display does not hold. Then, by compactness of the Cartesian product of the extended real line with the unit interval, there exists a subsequence $n'$ along which $d_n$ converges to a $c \in [0, \infty]$ and along which the probability in the previous display converges to a $\gamma \in (0, 1] $. Suppose first that $0 \leq c < \infty$. Then, from Equation \eqref{eqn:kappavb} and Assumption \eqref{eqn:maxto0}, we see that $\kappa_{n'}$, and hence $G_{n'}$, converges to $c$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and, by Equation \eqref{eqn:Hnbound}, that $H_{n'}$ converges to $0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, showing that $F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'}$ converges to $c \geq 0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and hence that the sequence in the previous display converges along $n'$ to $0<\gamma$, a contradiction. Assume next that $c = \infty$, and assume then, without loss of generality, that $d_{n'} > 0$ holds. We show that $(F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'})/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, which then again contradicts $\gamma \in (0, 1]$. Note that it suffices to verify that $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability. But this follows, because the expectation of $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ is $1$, and because, by relation~\eqref{eqn:kappavb}, its variance is bounded from above by \begin{equation} 4 d_{n'}^{-1} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n'} \mathbb{V}_{n'}(a_{i,n'})}{ \mathbb{V}_{n'}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n'} a_{i,n'})} \to 0, \end{equation} where we used $d_{n'} \to \infty$ and Assumption~\eqref{eqn:maxto0} to obtain the limit.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction along a subsequence with $d_n\to c$.

nodes.name: Extract subsequence
nodes.statement: Then, by compactness of the Cartesian product of the extended real line with the unit interval, there exists a subsequence $n'$ along which $d_n$ converges to a $c \in [0, \infty]$ and along which the probability in the previous display converges to a $\gamma \in (0, 1] $.
nodes.statement_short: Extract a subsequence with $d_{n'}\to c$ and probabilities $\to\gamma>0$.

nodes.name: Case $c<\infty$
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $0 \leq c < \infty$. Then, from Equation \eqref{eqn:kappavb} and Assumption \eqref{eqn:maxto0}, we see that $\kappa_{n'}$, and hence $G_{n'}$, converges to $c$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and, by Equation \eqref{eqn:Hnbound}, that $H_{n'}$ converges to $0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, showing that $F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'}$ converges to $c \geq 0$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, and hence that the sequence in the previous display converges along $n'$ to $0<\gamma$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Finite $c$: $F+G+H\to c\ge0$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Case $c=\infty$
nodes.statement: Assume next that $c = \infty$, and assume then, without loss of generality, that $d_{n'} > 0$ holds. We show that $(F_{n'} + G_{n'} + H_{n'})/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability, which then again contradicts $\gamma \in (0, 1]$. Note that it suffices to verify that $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ converges to $1$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n'}$-probability. But this follows, because the expectation of $\kappa_{n'}/d_{n'}$ is $1$, and because, by relation~\eqref{eqn:kappavb}, its variance is bounded from above by \begin{equation} 4 d_{n'}^{-1} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n'} \mathbb{V}_{n'}(a_{i,n'})}{ \mathbb{V}_{n'}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n'} a_{i,n'})} \to 0, \end{equation} where we used $d_{n'} \to \infty$ and Assumption~\eqref{eqn:maxto0} to obtain the limit.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2 (via Lemma C.1)
nodes.statement: We actually prove the following more detailed statement.

nodes.name: Detailed Gaussian approximation under Condition 1
nodes.statement: Under Condition \ref{cond:sum}, for $\varepsilon > 0$ we have \begin{align*} &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0, \\[7pt] &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \quad\text{and}\\[7pt] &\mathbb{P}_n \left(d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{align*} The last statement remains valid upon replacing $S_n$ by $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$ and then reduces to $d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{\dagger/2} \left(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_n^* \right)\right] , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)))\right) \to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Under Condition 1, diagonal and correlation of $S_n$ are consistent and the $S_n$-standardized error is close to $N(0,\mathrm{corr}(S_n))$.
nodes.label: lemma:equivSn:full

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma C.1
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma:nonstd} applied to the array $z_{i,n} = g_{i,n} \circ \pi_{i,n}$ defined on the space $({\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}, \mathcal{B}({\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}), \mathbb{P}_n)$, where $\pi_{i,n}: {\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell} \to {\mathbb R}^{1 \times \ell}$ extracts the $i-th$ row of an $n \times \ell$ matrix (to verify Condition~\ref{cond:zmomstd} we use Condition \ref{cond:sum} and replace the Lindeberg condition as discussed in Remark \ref{rem:lindeequiv}), shows that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we have \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0, \\ &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \end{align} and \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \hat{r}_{n,*} , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0, \end{equation} where $\hat{r}_{n, *} = \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} r_n$. The last part of Condition~\ref{cond:sum} together with Equation \eqref{eqn:varconvintro} now shows that $ \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \Delta_n \to 0$ w.r.t. $\mathbb{P}_n$, so that \begin{equation} \hat{r}_{n, *} = \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} \left( \hat{\theta}_n - \theta^*_n \right) + o_{\mathbb{P}_n}(1), \end{equation} which then proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma B.2 to $g_{i,n}\circ\pi_{i,n}$ and absorb the negligible remainder $\Delta_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.4
nodes.statement: For any (measurable) model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ we have \begin{align} & \mathbb{P}_n\left( \theta^{*(j)}_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1- \alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \\ \geq \quad & \mathbb{P}_n \left(\theta^{*(j)}_{\mathbb{M}, n} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \mathbb{M}}^{(j), \mathrm{est}} \text{ for all } \mathbb{M} \in \mathsf{M}_n \text{ and } j \in \{1, \hdots, m(\mathbb{M})\} \right). \end{align} It hence suffices to verify that the lower bound converges to $1-\alpha$. And for that (cf. Equation \eqref{eqn:hvarconv} below, and Condition \ref{cond:sum}) it suffices to verify that the following quantity converges to $1-\alpha$: \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \| \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n)^{\dagger/2} (\hat{\theta}_n - \theta^*_n) \|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_n)) \right). \end{equation} Lemma \ref{lemma:equivSn:full} shows that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we have \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \\ &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \\ &\mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \left[ \mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger/2} (\hat{\theta}_n - \theta^*_n) \right] , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(S_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon\right) \to 0. \end{align} This also shows that the two conditions imposed on $\hat{S}_n$ in the statement of the theorem are indeed equivalent. Furthermore, we immediately see that from any of these two assumptions, together with the previous display, it follows that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we have \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \\ &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( \hat{S}_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0 \\ &\mathbb{P}_n \left( d_w\left(\mathbb{P}_n \circ \bar{r}_{n, *} , N(0, \mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_n))\right) \geq \varepsilon\right) \to 0, \end{align} where $\bar{r}_{n, *} = \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n)^{\dagger/2} (\hat{\theta}_n - \theta^*_n)$. Next, let $n'$ be an arbitrary subsequence of $n$, and let $n''$ be a subsequence of $n'$ along which the norm-bounded sequence $\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))$ converges to $\bar{\Sigma}$, say. By \eqref{eqn:hcorrconv} it holds that $\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_{n''})$ converges to $\bar{\Sigma}$ in $\mathbb{P}_{n''}$-probability, and from the previous display it follows that $\mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ \bar{r}_{n'',*} \Rightarrow N(0, \bar{\Sigma})$. Combining these two statements, it then follows that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ (\bar{r}_{{n''}, *}, \mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_{n''})) \Rightarrow Q_{\bar{\Sigma}} \otimes \delta_{\bar{\Sigma}}, \end{equation} where $Q_{\bar{\Sigma}} := N(0, \bar{\Sigma})$, and where $\delta_{\bar{\Sigma}}$ denotes point mass at $\bar{\Sigma} \in {\mathbb R}^{k \times k}$. Now, define the map $F: {\mathbb R}^k \times {\mathbb R}^{k \times k}_{s, \geq 0}\to{\mathbb R}$ via $(z, \Sigma) \mapsto \|z\|_{\infty} - K_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma)$, where ${\mathbb R}^{k \times k}_{s, \geq 0}$ denotes the set of real, symmetric and nonnegative definite $k \times k$ dimensional matrices, and note that the map $F$ is continuous everywhere (cf. Lemma~\ref{lemma:POSIcont}). It follows from the continuous mapping theorem together with the previous display that \begin{equation} \mathbb{Q}_{n''} := \mathbb{P}_{n''} \circ F(\bar{r}_{{n''}, *}, \mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_{n''})) \Rightarrow Q_{\bar{\Sigma}} \circ \left(\|.\|_{\infty} - K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma})\right). \end{equation} Since the diagonal elements of $\bar{\Sigma}$ are ones (by its definition together with Condition \ref{cond:sum}), one can easily show that the $Q_{\bar{\Sigma}}$-probability of $\|.\|_{\infty} - K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma})$ being equal to $0$ is $0$. It hence follows from the Portmanteau theorem, together with the definition of $ K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma})$ and the previous display, that \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_{n''} \left( \| \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_{n''})^{\dagger/2} (\hat{\theta}_{n''} - \theta^*_{n''}) \|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\hat{S}_{n''})) \right) \\ = \quad &\mathbb{Q}_{n''} \left((-\infty, 0] \right) \to Q_{\bar{\Sigma}} \left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma})\right) = 1-\alpha. \end{align} This finishes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the max-statistic of all models; subsequence argument with Lemma C.1, continuity of $K_{1-\alpha}$ and the Portmanteau theorem.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:equivSn:full}, Lemma \ref{lemma:nonstd} applied to the array $z_{i,n} := g_{i,n} \circ \pi_{i,n}$ defined on $({\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}, \mathcal{B}({\mathbb R}^{n \times \ell}), \mathbb{P}_n)$ shows (in particular) that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{align} &\mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1} \mathrm{diag}(S_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{align} This shows that the two conditions given in the statement of the proposition are indeed equivalent, and, together with Condition \ref{cond:sum}, it also shows that for every $j = 1, \hdots, k$ we have $\mathbb{P}_n(\sum_{i = 1}^n [z^{(j)}_{i,n}]^2 = 0 ) \to 0$. Now, for $j = 1, \hdots, k$, we apply the first part of Lemma~\ref{lemma:auxi} (with $a_{i,n} = g^{(j)}_{i,n} \circ \pi_{i,n}$ and $b_{i,n} = \hat{g}^{(j)}_{i,n}$) to obtain for every $\varepsilon > 0$ that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{diag}(S_n)^{\dagger} \mathrm{diag}(\hat{S}_n) - I_k\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Next, we can, in a similar way, apply the second part of Lemma \ref{lemma:auxi} to obtain \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \|\mathrm{corr} \left( \hat{S}_n \right) - \mathrm{corr} \left( S_n \right)\| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} This finishes the proof. \hfill\qed

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.6
nodes.statement: Similarly as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fbl} we now need to verify that \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \| \mathrm{diag}(\hat{\nu}^2_n)^{\dagger/2} \left[r_n + \Delta_n \right]\|_{\infty} \leq \hat{K}_n \right) \geq 1- \alpha. \end{equation} We make the following preparatory observation: Denote the event on which $\kappa_n$ is well defined by $A_n$ (recall that $\mathbb{P}_n(A_n) \to 1$), and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Observe that the limit inferior in Equation \eqref{eqn:statem} is not smaller than \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \kappa_n \| \mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1/2} \left[r_n + \Delta_n \right] \|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))), A_n \right), \end{equation} which, in turn, is bounded from below (using that $\kappa_n$ is positive on $A_n$, and Equation \eqref{eqn:asptup}) by \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \| \mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))^{-1/2} \left[r_n + \Delta_n \right] \|_{\infty} \leq \frac{K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)))}{1 + \varepsilon} \right). \end{equation} Now, we argue by contradiction, and suppose that \eqref{eqn:statem} is false: Then there exists a $\delta > 0$, that can be chosen independently of $\varepsilon$, so that the limit inferior in \eqref{eq:liminfbd} is an element of $[0, 1-\alpha - \delta)$. Next, let $n'(\varepsilon)$ denote a subsequence along which \eqref{eq:liminfbd} is attained. Arguing as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fbl} (borrowing some of its notation) we can obtain a subsequence $n''(\varepsilon)$ of $n'(\varepsilon)$ along which the sequence of probabilities in the preceding display converges to \begin{align} Q_{\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon)}\left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq \frac{K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon))}{1+\varepsilon} \right) \in [0, 1-\alpha - \delta). \end{align} Note that $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, and let $\varepsilon_m > 0$ converge to $0$. Assume (otherwise pass to a subsequence) that the sequence of correlation matrices $\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m)$ (with diagonal entries equal to $1$) converges to $\bar{\Sigma}$, say. It is then not difficult to obtain (by a weak convergence argument involving Portmanteau theorem) the contradiction \begin{align} & Q_{\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m)}\left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq \frac{K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m))}{1+\varepsilon_m} \right) \\ &\xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{} \quad Q_{\bar{\Sigma}}\left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma}) \right) = 1-\alpha. \end{align} The remaining part follows immediately from what we have already established. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound the coverage via $\kappa_n$, then argue by contradiction along subsequences as in Theorem 2.4.

Assume (otherwise pass to a subsequence) that the sequence of correlation matrices $\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m)$ (with diagonal entries equal to $1$) converges to $\bar{\Sigma}$, say. It is then not difficult to obtain (by a weak convergence argument involving Portmanteau theorem) the contradiction \begin{align} & Q_{\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m)}\left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq \frac{K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma}(\varepsilon_m))}{1+\varepsilon_m} \right) \\ &\xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{} \quad Q_{\bar{\Sigma}}\left(y \in {\mathbb R}^k: \|y\|_{\infty} \leq K_{1-\alpha}(\bar{\Sigma}) \right) = 1-\alpha. \end{align} The remaining part follows immediately from what we have already established. \hfill\qed

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.7
nodes.statement: Fix $j$ and note that with the same notation and argumentation as in the beginning of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:obtest}, and with the convention of Remark~\ref{rem:gin}, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\left|\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n [g_{i,n}^{(j)}]^2}{\sum_{i = 1}^n \mathbb{V}_n(g_{i,n}^{(j)})} - 1 \right| \geq \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Obviously, \begin{equation} \tilde{g}_{i,n}^{(j)} = \left( \hat{g}_{i,n}^{(j)} - g_{i,n}^{(j)}\right) + g_{i,n}^{(j)} + a_{i,n}^{(j)}. \end{equation} Equation~\eqref{eq:negldiff}, or equivalently (equivalence being due to Equation~\eqref{eqn:overest1} above) Equation~\eqref{eq:negldiff2}, together with Part~3 of Lemma~\ref{lemma:auxi} (applied with: $a_{i,n} = g_{i,n}^{(j)}$, $b_{i,n} = \left( \hat{g}_{i,n}^{(j)} - g_{i,n}^{(j)}\right) + g_{i,n}^{(j)}$ and $c_{i,n} = a_{i,n}^{(j)}$) now shows that \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n [\tilde{g}_{i,n}^{(j)}]^2 }{\sum_{i = 1}^n \mathbb{V}_n(g_{i,n}^{(j)})} \leq 1-\varepsilon \right) \to 0 \text{ for every } \varepsilon > 0, \end{equation} implying the claimed statement. Note that Equation~\eqref{eqn:maxto0} in Lemma~\ref{lemma:auxi} is satisfied here because Condition~\ref{cond:sum} (in particular the Lindeberg condition in Equation \eqref{eq:linde}) implies the corresponding Feller condition \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, {n}} \mathbb{V}_{n}(g_{i,{n}}^{(j)})}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \mathbb{V}_{n}(g_{i,{n}}^{(j)})} \to 0. \end{equation} All remaining assumptions in Part 3 of Lemma \ref{lemma:auxi} can be easily checked using Condition~\ref{cond:sum}, \eqref{eq:negldiff} and \eqref{eqn:overest1}. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\tilde g$ and apply Part 3 of Lemma B.4, with the Feller condition from Lindeberg.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.9
nodes.statement: Let $\omega := \mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)$ and let $Z \sim N(0, \Gamma)$. Since $\Gamma$ is a correlation matrix of rank $\omega$, by the spectral decomposition, we can find a $k \times \omega$-dimensional matrix $V$ so that $VV' = \Gamma$. In particular if $\varepsilon \sim N(0, I_{\omega})$ it holds that $V \varepsilon \sim N(0, \Gamma)$, and hence the $1-\alpha$-quantiles of the distributions of $\|Z\|_{\infty}$ and of $\| V\varepsilon\|_{\infty} = \max_{i = 1, \hdots, k } |v_i \varepsilon |$ coincide, $v_i$ denoting the $i$-th row of $V$. Since $\Gamma$ is a correlation matrix it furthermore holds that each row $v_i$ of $V$ has Euclidean norm less than or equal to $1$. From the discussion after the definition of $B_{\alpha}$ it then follows that $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$, the $1-\alpha$-quantile of the distributions of $\|Z\|_{\infty}$, is not greater than $B_{\alpha}(\omega, k)$. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Factor $\Gamma=VV'$ with rows of norm at most one and apply the defining property of $B_\alpha$.

nodes.statement_short: Factor $\Gamma=VV'$ with $V$ of rank $\omega$.

nodes.statement_short: Represent $Z$ as $V\varepsilon$.

nodes.statement_short: Rows of $V$ have norm at most one.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: From the discussion after the definition of $B_{\alpha}$ it then follows that $K_{1-\alpha}(\Gamma)$, the $1-\alpha$-quantile of the distributions of $\|Z\|_{\infty}$, is not greater than $B_{\alpha}(\omega, k)$. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply the defining bound of $B_\alpha$.

Abbreviate $m = |M|$, $u_n = u_n(y) = y - \mu_n$ and $H_M = I_n-P_{X_n[M]}$. The mean of $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2(y) = (n-m)^{-1} y'H_My$ is easily seen to be ${\mathbb E}_n[\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2] = \mu_n'H_M\mu_n/(n-m) + \sigma_n^2$, eventually. Now consider  egin{align} &\left| rac{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2}{{\mathbb E}_n[\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2]} - 1ight| \quad=\quad \left| rac{2\mu_nH_M u_n/(n-m) + u_n'H_M u_n/(n-m) - \sigma_n^2}{\mu_n' H_M \mu_n/(n-m) + \sigma_n^2}ight|

e j} (H_M)_{ij} v_{i,n}v_{j,n}, $$ and note that $(n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i
e j} (H_M)_{ij} v_{i,n}v_{j,n}$ has mean zero and variance equal to $(n-m)^{-2}\sum_{i
e j} [(H_M)_{ij}]^2\le (n-m)^{-2}\mathrm{trace}(H_M^2) = (n-m)^{-1}	o0$. To show that $(n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (H_M)_{ii} v_{i,n}^2$ converges to one, we use a standard truncation argument. nodes.name: Off-diagonal part
nodes.statement:
To show that the second fraction converges to one, abbreviate the random $n$-vector $v_n = u_n/\sigma_n$, and note that $v_n$ has independent standardized components under ${\mathbb P}_n$. Now decompose the quadratic form as $$  rac{v_n'H_Mv_n}{n-m} \quad=\quad  rac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^n (H_M)_{ii} v_{i,n}^2 +  rac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i
e j} (H_M)_{ij} v_{i,n}v_{j,n}, $$ and note that $(n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i
e j} (H_M)_{ij} v_{i,n}v_{j,n}$ has mean zero and variance equal to $(n-m)^{-2}\sum_{i
e j} [(H_M)_{ij}]^2\le (n-m)^{-2}\mathrm{trace}(H_M^2) = (n-m)^{-1}	o0$.
nodes.statement_short: Off-diagonal quadratic form has vanishing variance.

nodes.name: Truncation
nodes.statement: To show that $(n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (H_M)_{ii} v_{i,n}^2$ converges to one, we use a standard truncation argument. For $K>0$ define $\tilde{v}_{i,n} = v_{i,n}\{|v_{i,n}|\le K\}$, $S_n = \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^n(H_M)_{ii} v_{i,n}^2$, $\tilde{S}_n = \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^n(H_M)_{ii} \tilde{v}_{i,n}^2$ and \begin{align*} D_n &:= S_n - \tilde{S}_n = \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^n(H_M)_{ii} v_{i,n}^2\{|v_{i,n}|>K\} \;\ge\; 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Truncate at level $K$.

nodes.name: Remainder bound
nodes.statement: Using first H\"older's inequality, and then Markov's inequality (recall that $\mathbb{E}(v^2_{i,n}) = 1$), $\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \left({\mathbb E}_n[|v_{i,n}|^{2+\delta}]\right)^{2/(2+\delta)} \leq \tau$ (recall that ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta,\tau)$), and $\mathrm{trace}(H_M) = n-m$, the mean of $D_n$ can be bounded by \begin{align*} {\mathbb E}_n[D_n] &\le \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^n(H_M)_{ii} \left({\mathbb E}_n[|v_{i,n}|^{2+\delta}]\right)^{2/(2+\delta)}{\mathbb P}_n(|v_{i,n}|^2>K^2)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}\\ &\le \tau K^{-\frac{2\delta}{2+\delta}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the truncation remainder by $\tau K^{-2\delta/(2+\delta)}$.

nodes.name: Diagonal part converges
nodes.statement: Now for $\varepsilon>0$, \begin{align*} &{\mathbb P}_n(|S_n-1|>\varepsilon) \\ &\quad\le {\mathbb P}_n(|S_n-\tilde{S}_n|>\varepsilon/2) + {\mathbb P}_n(|\tilde{S}_n- {\mathbb E}_n[\tilde{S}_n] + {\mathbb E}_n[\tilde{S}_n]-1|>\varepsilon/2)\\ &\quad\le 2\tau K^{-\frac{2\delta}{2+\delta}}/\varepsilon + 16{\mathbb V}_n[\tilde{S}_n]/\varepsilon^2 + {\mathbb P}_n(\tau K^{-\frac{2\delta}{2+\delta}}>\varepsilon/4). \end{align*} Since the variance of $\tilde{S}_n$ clearly converges to zero as $n\to\infty$, for every $K>0$, the limit superior of ${\mathbb P}_n(|S_n-1|>\varepsilon)$ is bounded by a quantity that approaches zero as $K\to\infty$. Thus, we have established the convergence $\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2/{\mathbb E}_n[\hat{\sigma}_{M,n}^2] \to 1$, in ${\mathbb P}_n$-probability.
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev plus remainder bound; let $K\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can write \begin{align*} \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2}{\sigma_n^2} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2}{{\mathbb E}_n[\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2]} \frac{{\mathbb E}_n[\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2]}{\sigma_n^2} = (1+o_{{\mathbb P}_n}(1)) \left( \frac{(\mu_n/\sigma_n)'H_M(\mu_n/\sigma_n)}{n-m} + 1 \right), \end{align*} which finishes the proof.\hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Combine ratios.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement: For every $n \in {\mathbb N}$, let $\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$. Abbreviate $u_{i,n}(y_i) := y_i - \mu_{i,n}$, and $u_n(y) = (u_{1,n}(y_1), \hdots, u_{n,n}(y_n))'$, where $y=(y_1,\dots, y_n)'\in{\mathbb R}^n$ and $\mu_n = (\mu_{1,n},\dots, \mu_{n,n})'$. We note that by assumption \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}_{i,n} (|u_{i,n}|^{2+\delta})^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}}}{\sigma_n^2} \leq \tau. \end{equation} We now verify Condition \ref{cond:sum} (with $\Delta_n \equiv 0$): Since this condition is formulated in a component-wise fashion, it suffices to verify it for an arbitrary component $j\in\{1,\dots, m(\mathbb M)\}$ of the estimation error $r_{n,\mathbb M}$ in an arbitrary model $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$ with corresponding index set $M\in\mathcal I$. Recall that \begin{equation} \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*} = \left(X_n[M]' X_n[M] \right)^{-1} X_n[M]'\mu_n = U_n^{-1} X_n[M]'\mu_n, \end{equation} for $U_n := X_n[M]' X_n[M] $. The $j$-th coordinate of the estimation error \begin{equation} r_{n,\mathbb M}(y) \;:=\; \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y) - \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*} = U_n^{-1}X_n[M]'u_n(y) \end{equation} can be written as \begin{equation} \sum_{i = 1}^n e_{|M|}'(j)U_n^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' u_{i,n}(y_i) =: \sum_{i=1}^n g^{(j)}_{i,n,\mathbb M}(y_i), \end{equation} where $e_m(j)$ denotes the $j$-th element of the canonical basis of ${\mathbb R}^m$. By definition $\mathbb{E}_{i,n} \left( g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} \right) = 0$ and $0 < \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} \right) < \infty$ holds (eventually), the latter following from \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M} \right) = \sigma_n^2 U_n^{-1} \end{equation} together with Condition~\ref{cond:X}. We now verify that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n^{-1}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \sum_{i = 1}^n \int_{\mathbb R} \left[ g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right]^2 \left\{ |g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}| \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right\} d \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \to 0. \end{equation} An application of H\"older's inequality (with $p = \frac{2+\delta}{2}$ and $q = \frac{2+\delta}{\delta}$) shows that the quantity to the left in the previous display is bounded from above by \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}_{i,n} (|u_{i,n}|^{2+\delta})^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}}}{\sigma_n^2}\left( \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \left( | g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} | \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right) \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} , \end{equation} which, using the bound \eqref{eqn:astau} and Markov's inequality, does not exceed \begin{equation} \tau ~ \left( \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \left( U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}\right)_{j} }{ \left( U_n^{-1}\right)_{j}} \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} ~ \varepsilon^{-\frac{2\delta}{2 + \delta}} . \end{equation} Finally, since the term within brackets coincides with \begin{equation} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \bigg( X_{i,n}[M] U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{W_{j,n}}{\|W_{j,n}\|} U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} X_{i,n}[M]' \bigg), \end{equation} for \begin{align} W_{j,n} = U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} e_{|M|}(j) e'_{|M|}(j) U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \end{align} and since this quantity is not greater than \begin{equation} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \to 0, \end{equation} where convergence holds by Condition \ref{cond:X}, the statement in \eqref{eqn:lindehomreg} follows. Since $\mathbb M$ and $j$ were arbitrary, we have verified Condition~\ref{cond:sum}. Now, for $\mathbb M$, $M$ and $j$ as before, set $\hat{\nu}_{j,n,\mathbb M}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2 (U_n^{-1})_{j}$. Thus, using \eqref{eqn:varhomlin} and Proposition~\ref{prop:lmvarest}, we see that \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \sqrt{ \frac{[\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M})]_j }{\hat{\nu}_{j,n,\mathbb M}^2 }} \geq 1+\varepsilon \right) = \mathbb{P}_n \left( \sqrt{ \frac{\sigma_n^2 }{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2 } } \geq 1+\varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{align*} Finally, note that for the stacked vector $r_n = (r_{n,\mathbb M_1}',\dots, r_{n,\mathbb M_d}')'$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) = \sigma_n^2 \Gamma_n, \end{equation} and that $K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)) = K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))) > 0$. It now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:cons} (the special case with $\hat{K}_n = K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n))$, that for any (measurable) model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ it holds that \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{*, (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation} The theorem now follows because the selection $\mathbb{P}_n$ we started with was arbitrary. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Verify Condition 1 for OLS (Lindeberg via Hoelder and leverage), show $\hat\sigma^2$ overestimates via Proposition 3.4, then apply Theorem 2.6.

nodes.statement: For every $n \in {\mathbb N}$, let $\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$. Abbreviate $u_{i,n}(y_i) := y_i - \mu_{i,n}$, and $u_n(y) = (u_{1,n}(y_1), \hdots, u_{n,n}(y_n))'$, where $y=(y_1,\dots, y_n)'\in{\mathbb R}^n$ and $\mu_n = (\mu_{1,n},\dots, \mu_{n,n})'$. The $j$-th coordinate of the estimation error \begin{equation} r_{n,\mathbb M}(y) \;:=\; \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y) - \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*} = U_n^{-1}X_n[M]'u_n(y) \end{equation} can be written as \begin{equation} \sum_{i = 1}^n e_{|M|}'(j)U_n^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' u_{i,n}(y_i) =: \sum_{i=1}^n g^{(j)}_{i,n,\mathbb M}(y_i), \end{equation} where $e_m(j)$ denotes the $j$-th element of the canonical basis of ${\mathbb R}^m$.

nodes.name: Equation (D.3)
nodes.statement: \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*} = \left(X_n[M]' X_n[M] \right)^{-1} X_n[M]'\mu_n = U_n^{-1} X_n[M]'\mu_n,

nodes.name: Equation (D.4)
nodes.statement: r_{n,\mathbb M}(y) \;:=\; \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y) - \beta_{\mathbb{M}, n}^{*} = U_n^{-1}X_n[M]'u_n(y)

nodes.statement: By definition $\mathbb{E}_{i,n} \left( g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} \right) = 0$ and $0 < \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} \right) < \infty$ holds (eventually), the latter following from \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M} \right) = \sigma_n^2 U_n^{-1} \end{equation} together with Condition~\ref{cond:X}.

nodes.name: Equation (D.6) [eqn:varhomlin]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M} \right) = \sigma_n^2 U_n^{-1}
nodes.label: eqn:varhomlin

nodes.name: Lindeberg condition
nodes.statement: We now verify that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ it holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n^{-1}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \sum_{i = 1}^n \int_{\mathbb R} \left[ g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right]^2 \left\{ |g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}| \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right\} d \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \to 0. \end{equation} An application of H\"older's inequality (with $p = \frac{2+\delta}{2}$ and $q = \frac{2+\delta}{\delta}$) shows that the quantity to the left in the previous display is bounded from above by \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}_{i,n} (|u_{i,n}|^{2+\delta})^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}}}{\sigma_n^2}\left( \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \left( | g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} | \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right) \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} , \end{equation} which, using the bound \eqref{eqn:astau} and Markov's inequality, does not exceed \begin{equation} \tau ~ \left( \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \left( U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}\right)_{j} }{ \left( U_n^{-1}\right)_{j}} \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} ~ \varepsilon^{-\frac{2\delta}{2 + \delta}} . \end{equation} Finally, since the term within brackets coincides with \begin{equation} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \bigg( X_{i,n}[M] U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{W_{j,n}}{\|W_{j,n}\|} U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} X_{i,n}[M]' \bigg), \end{equation} for \begin{align} W_{j,n} = U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} e_{|M|}(j) e'_{|M|}(j) U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \end{align} and since this quantity is not greater than \begin{equation} \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \to 0, \end{equation} where convergence holds by Condition \ref{cond:X}, the statement in \eqref{eqn:lindehomreg} follows. Since $\mathbb M$ and $j$ were arbitrary, we have verified Condition~\ref{cond:sum}.
nodes.statement_short: Lindeberg via Hoelder, Markov and the leverage condition.

nodes.name: Equation (D.7) [eqn:lindehomreg]
nodes.statement: \mathbb{V}_n^{-1}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \sum_{i = 1}^n \int_{\mathbb R} \left[ g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right]^2 \left\{ |g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}| \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right\} d \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \to 0.
nodes.label: eqn:lindehomreg

nodes.name: Equation (D.8)
nodes.statement: \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}_{i,n} (|u_{i,n}|^{2+\delta})^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}}}{\sigma_n^2}\left( \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{P}_{i,n} \left( | g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} | \geq \varepsilon \mathbb{V}_n^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right) \right) \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} ,

nodes.name: Equation (D.9) [eq:thm:homlinmods:w2]
nodes.statement: \tau ~ \left( \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \left( U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}\right)_{j} }{ \left( U_n^{-1}\right)_{j}} \right)^{\frac{\delta}{2 + \delta}} ~ \varepsilon^{-\frac{2\delta}{2 + \delta}} .
nodes.label: eq:thm:homlinmods:w2

nodes.name: Equation (D.10)
nodes.statement: \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \bigg( X_{i,n}[M] U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{W_{j,n}}{\|W_{j,n}\|} U_n^{-\frac{1}{2}} X_{i,n}[M]' \bigg),

nodes.name: Equation (D.12)
nodes.statement: \max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1} X_{i,n}[M]' \to 0,

nodes.name: Overestimation
nodes.statement: Now, for $\mathbb M$, $M$ and $j$ as before, set $\hat{\nu}_{j,n,\mathbb M}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2 (U_n^{-1})_{j}$. Thus, using \eqref{eqn:varhomlin} and Proposition~\ref{prop:lmvarest}, we see that \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}_n \left( \sqrt{ \frac{[\mathbb{V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M})]_j }{\hat{\nu}_{j,n,\mathbb M}^2 }} \geq 1+\varepsilon \right) = \mathbb{P}_n \left( \sqrt{ \frac{\sigma_n^2 }{\hat{\sigma}_{\mathbb M,n}^2 } } \geq 1+\varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.4 shows the variance estimator overestimates.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, note that for the stacked vector $r_n = (r_{n,\mathbb M_1}',\dots, r_{n,\mathbb M_d}')'$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) = \sigma_n^2 \Gamma_n, \end{equation} and that $K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n)) = K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))) > 0$. It now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:cons} (the special case with $\hat{K}_n = K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Gamma_n))$, that for any (measurable) model selection procedure $\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n$ it holds that \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{*, (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha. \end{equation} The theorem now follows because the selection $\mathbb{P}_n$ we started with was arbitrary. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply the special case of Theorem 2.6.

nodes.name: Equation (D.13)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{V}_n(r_n) = \sigma_n^2 \Gamma_n,

nodes.name: Equation (D.14)
nodes.statement: \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{*, (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{lm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement: The proof is analogous to that of Theorem~\ref{thm:homlinmods}, with the only modification that throughout $j=1$ and that the stacked vector $r_n$ is now given by $r_n = (r_{n,\mathbb M_1}^{(1)},\dots, r_{n,\mathbb M_d}^{(1)})'$, so that $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n) = \sigma_n^2 \Xi_n$ and thus $K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\Xi_n)) = K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))) > 0$.\hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: As for Theorem 3.2 with only first coordinates stacked, so that $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)=\sigma_n^2\Xi_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.5
nodes.statement: We argue by contradiction, and assume existence of a sequence of measurable functions $(\hat{\sigma}^2_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\hat{\sigma}^2_{n}: \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, \infty)$ and so that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ Equation \eqref{eqn:conscounter} holds. First, we define for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $\rho \geq 0$ the product measure \begin{equation} Q_n(x, \rho) = \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \bigg( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho)\bigg), \end{equation} where $Q(x_i)$ puts mass $1/2$ to $x_i + 1$ and to $x_i - 1$, respectively, and $Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho)$ denotes the convolution of $Q(x_i)$ and $N(0, \rho)$, where we interpret $N(0, 0)$ as point mass at $0$, i.e., $Q(x_i) \ast N(0, 0) = Q(x_i)$. For simplicity, denote the $q$-th absolute central moment of a distribution $F$ on the Borel sets of ${\mathbb R}$ by $m_q(F)$. We note that $Q_n(x, 0) \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$, because $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i))^{\frac{2}{2+h}} = 1$ for every $h \geq 0$, and since $\tau > 1$ holds by assumption. It is easy to verify that for every $h \geq 0$ the quantity $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho) )^{\frac{2}{2+h}}$ does not depend on $x_i$, and that we have $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho) )^{\frac{2}{2+h}} \to 1$ as $\rho \to 0$. Hence there exists a $\rho^* > 0$, so that for every $\rho \in[0,\rho^*]$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ we have $Q_n(x, \rho) \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$. Therefore, by our assumption, it holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$ that \begin{equation} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \sup_{0 \leq \rho \le \rho^*} ~ Q_n(x, \rho) \left( \bigg | \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_n}{1 + \rho} - 1 \bigg | > \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation} Next, let $(F, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{Q})$ be a probability space on which, for every $n$, there are defined two independent random $n$-vectors $X_n^{(1)}$ and $X_n^{(2)}$, so that $\mathbb{Q} \circ X_n^{(1)} \sim Q_n(0, 0)$ and $\mathbb{Q} \circ X_n^{(2)} \sim N(0, \rho^*I_n)$, and hence the distribution of $Y_n := X_n^{(1)} + X_n^{(2)}$ is $Q_n(0, \rho^*)$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be fixed. From the previous display it follows that $\mathbb{Q}(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n(Y_n) - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon )$ converges to $0$. Since the conditional distribution of $Y_n$ given $X_n^{(2)}$ is $Q_n(X_n^{(2)}, 0)$, it furthermore holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{Q}(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n(Y_n) - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}} \left( Q_n(X_n^{(2)}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon )\right) \to 0, \end{equation} from which it now follows that $I_n(\omega) = Q_n(X_n^{(2)}(\omega), 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$ in $\mathbb{Q}$-probability as $n \to \infty$. Thus, there exists a subsequence $n'$ so that $I_{n'} \to 0$, $\mathbb{Q}$-almost surely. As a consequence, there exists $\bar{\omega} \in \Omega$ for which $I_{n'}(\bar{\omega}) \to 0$ as $n' \to \infty$. But this now means that for $x_{n'} = X_{n'}^{(2)}(\bar{\omega})$ it holds that $Q_{n'}(x_{n'}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_{n'} - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$. Since $\rho^* > 0$, this contradicts Equation \eqref{eqn:contra} which implies $Q_{n'}(x_{n'}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_{n'} - 1 | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: Rademacher-plus-Gaussian product measures with variances $1$ and $1+\rho^*$ cannot both be estimated consistently by conditioning on the Gaussian part.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement: We argue by contradiction, and assume existence of a sequence of measurable functions $(\hat{\sigma}^2_{n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\hat{\sigma}^2_{n}: \mathbb{R}^n \to [0, \infty)$ and so that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ Equation \eqref{eqn:conscounter} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a uniformly consistent estimator.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.statement: First, we define for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $\rho \geq 0$ the product measure \begin{equation} Q_n(x, \rho) = \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \bigg( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho)\bigg), \end{equation} where $Q(x_i)$ puts mass $1/2$ to $x_i + 1$ and to $x_i - 1$, respectively, and $Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho)$ denotes the convolution of $Q(x_i)$ and $N(0, \rho)$, where we interpret $N(0, 0)$ as point mass at $0$, i.e., $Q(x_i) \ast N(0, 0) = Q(x_i)$. For simplicity, denote the $q$-th absolute central moment of a distribution $F$ on the Borel sets of ${\mathbb R}$ by $m_q(F)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define Rademacher-Gaussian convolution product measures $Q_n(x,\rho)$.

nodes.name: Equation (D.15)
nodes.statement: Q_n(x, \rho) = \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \bigg( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho)\bigg),

nodes.name: Membership
nodes.statement: We note that $Q_n(x, 0) \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$, because $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i))^{\frac{2}{2+h}} = 1$ for every $h \geq 0$, and since $\tau > 1$ holds by assumption. It is easy to verify that for every $h \geq 0$ the quantity $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho) )^{\frac{2}{2+h}}$ does not depend on $x_i$, and that we have $m_{2+h}( Q(x_i) \ast N(0, \rho) )^{\frac{2}{2+h}} \to 1$ as $\rho \to 0$. Hence there exists a $\rho^* > 0$, so that for every $\rho \in[0,\rho^*]$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ we have $Q_n(x, \rho) \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{lm})}(\delta, \tau)$. Therefore, by our assumption, it holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$ that \begin{equation} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \sup_{0 \leq \rho \le \rho^*} ~ Q_n(x, \rho) \left( \bigg | \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_n}{1 + \rho} - 1 \bigg | > \varepsilon \right) \to 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: These measures lie in the feasible set for small $\rho$, so the estimator is consistent for $1+\rho$.

nodes.name: Equation (D.16) [eqn:contra]
nodes.statement: \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \sup_{0 \leq \rho \le \rho^*} ~ Q_n(x, \rho) \left( \bigg | \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_n}{1 + \rho} - 1 \bigg | > \varepsilon \right) \to 0.
nodes.label: eqn:contra

nodes.name: Coupling
nodes.statement: Next, let $(F, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{Q})$ be a probability space on which, for every $n$, there are defined two independent random $n$-vectors $X_n^{(1)}$ and $X_n^{(2)}$, so that $\mathbb{Q} \circ X_n^{(1)} \sim Q_n(0, 0)$ and $\mathbb{Q} \circ X_n^{(2)} \sim N(0, \rho^*I_n)$, and hence the distribution of $Y_n := X_n^{(1)} + X_n^{(2)}$ is $Q_n(0, \rho^*)$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be fixed. From the previous display it follows that $\mathbb{Q}(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n(Y_n) - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon )$ converges to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Couple $Y_n=X^{(1)}+X^{(2)}$ with law $Q_n(0,\rho^*)$.

nodes.name: Conditioning
nodes.statement: Since the conditional distribution of $Y_n$ given $X_n^{(2)}$ is $Q_n(X_n^{(2)}, 0)$, it furthermore holds that \begin{equation} \mathbb{Q}(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n(Y_n) - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}} \left( Q_n(X_n^{(2)}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon )\right) \to 0, \end{equation} from which it now follows that $I_n(\omega) = Q_n(X_n^{(2)}(\omega), 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$ in $\mathbb{Q}$-probability as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the Gaussian part.

nodes.name: Equation (D.17)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{Q}(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n(Y_n) - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}} \left( Q_n(X_n^{(2)}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_n - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon )\right) \to 0,

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Thus, there exists a subsequence $n'$ so that $I_{n'} \to 0$, $\mathbb{Q}$-almost surely. As a consequence, there exists $\bar{\omega} \in \Omega$ for which $I_{n'}(\bar{\omega}) \to 0$ as $n' \to \infty$. But this now means that for $x_{n'} = X_{n'}^{(2)}(\bar{\omega})$ it holds that $Q_{n'}(x_{n'}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_{n'} - (1 + \rho^*) | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$. Since $\rho^* > 0$, this contradicts Equation \eqref{eqn:contra} which implies $Q_{n'}(x_{n'}, 0)(|\hat{\sigma}^2_{n'} - 1 | > \varepsilon ) \to 0$. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Almost sure subsequence yields conflicting limits $1$ and $1+\rho^*$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.6
nodes.statement: We proceed as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:homlinmods}, noting that now we allow for heteroskedasticity, so that $\sigma_{i,n}^2 = \mathbb{V}_{i,n}(u_{i,n})$ depends on $i$. The bound \eqref{eqn:astau} in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:homlinmods} is now replaced by \begin{equation} \frac{\max_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \mathbb{E}_{i,n} (|u_{i,n}|^{2+\delta})^{\frac{2}{2+\delta}}}{\min_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \sigma_{i,n}^2} \leq \tau. \end{equation} To verify Condition \ref{cond:sum} we replace \eqref{eqn:varhomlin} in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:homlinmods} by \begin{align} \mathbb{V}_{n} \left( r_{n,\mathbb M} \right) = U_n^{-1} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^n \sigma_{i,n}^2 X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M] \right)U_n^{-1} \end{align} which, replacing each $\sigma_{i,n}^2$ by $\min_{i = 1, \hdots, n} \sigma_{i,n}^2 > 0$, is seen to be eventually positive by Condition~\ref{cond:X}. For the verification of the Lindeberg condition \eqref{eqn:lindehomreg} we use essentially the same argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:homlinmods}, now using \eqref{eqn:astauhet} above. Hence, Condition~\ref{cond:sum} holds. Next, we verify \eqref{eqn:special2} in Theorem~\ref{thm:cons} by means of Proposition~\ref{prop:overest}. Let \begin{align*} &\tilde{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}(y) = U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'\hat{u}_{i,\mathbb M}(y) \\ &\quad= U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'\left( u_{i,n}(y_i) + X_{i,n}(\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^* - \hat{\beta}_{\mathbb M,n}(y)) + \mu_{i,n}-X_{i,n}[M]\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\right)\\ &\quad= \hat{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}(y) + a_{i,n,\mathbb M}, \end{align*} where $\hat{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M} = U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'u_{i,n} - U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]r_{n,\mathbb M}$ and $a_{i,n,\mathbb M}= U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'(\mu_{i,n}-X_{i,n}[M]\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*)\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$, and recall that $g_{i,n,\mathbb M} = U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'u_{i,n}$. Therefore, $$ \hat{\nu}_{j,\mathbb M,n}^2 := \hat{\sigma}_{j,\mathbb M,n}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\tilde{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right]^2, $$ and, from \eqref{eqn:varhetlin}, \begin{align*} &{\mathbb E}_n\left(g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} - \hat{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right)^2 = \left[U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]{\mathbb V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M})X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}\right]_j \\ &\quad\le (e_{|M|}(j)'U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]')^2 \left(\max_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2\right) \max_{i=1,\dots, n}X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'. \end{align*} Moreover, $\sum_{i=1}^n {\mathbb V}_n(g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)})={\mathbb V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}) \ge [U_n^{-1}]_j\min_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2 $. Thus, \eqref{eq:negldiff2} follows, because $$ \sum_{i=1}^n(e_{|M|}(j)'U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]')^2 = [U_n^{-1}]_j \quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\max_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2}{\min_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2}\le \tau, $$ in view of \eqref{eqn:astauhet}, and, finally, because of Condition~\ref{cond:X}. Consequently, Proposition~\ref{prop:overest} implies \eqref{eqn:special2} for the proposed variance estimators. If $r_n$ is now, again, the stacked vector of the $r_{n,\mathbb M_1},\dots, r_{n,\mathbb M_d}$, then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:upper}, we have that $B_{\alpha}(\min(k, p),k) \geq K_{1-\alpha}(\mathrm{corr}(\mathbb{V}_n(r_n))) > 0$ (it is easy to see that the rank of the $k \times k$-dimensional matrix $\mathbb{V}_n(r_n)$ can not exceed $p$), so we can apply the special case discussed in Theorem~\ref{thm:cons} to conclude that \begin{equation} \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_n \left(\beta_{\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n, n}^{*, (j)} \in \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha, \hat{\mathbb{M}}_n}^{(j), \mathrm{hlm}} \text{ for all } j = 1, \hdots, m(\hat{\mathbb{M}}_n) \right) \geq 1-\alpha, \end{equation} which proves the claim as the sequence $\mathbb{P}_n \in \mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{het})}(\delta, \tau)$ was arbitrary.\hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: As for Theorem 3.2 with heteroskedastic variances; Eicker estimator overestimates via Proposition 2.7; POSI constant bounded by Lemma 2.9.

nodes.statement: Therefore, $$ \hat{\nu}_{j,\mathbb M,n}^2 := \hat{\sigma}_{j,\mathbb M,n}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\tilde{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right]^2, $$ and, from \eqref{eqn:varhetlin}, \begin{align*} &{\mathbb E}_n\left(g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)} - \hat{g}_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}\right)^2 = \left[U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]{\mathbb V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M})X_{i,n}[M]'X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}\right]_j \\ &\quad\le (e_{|M|}(j)'U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]')^2 \left(\max_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2\right) \max_{i=1,\dots, n}X_{i,n}[M]U_n^{-1}X_{i,n}[M]'. \end{align*} Moreover, $\sum_{i=1}^n {\mathbb V}_n(g_{i,n,\mathbb M}^{(j)})={\mathbb V}_n(r_{n,\mathbb M}^{(j)}) \ge [U_n^{-1}]_j\min_{i=1,\dots, n}\sigma_{i,n}^2 $.

Consequently, Proposition~\ref{prop:overest} implies \eqref{eqn:special2} for the proposed variance estimators.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.1
nodes.statement: We begin by establishing the following preliminary result. For every pair $(h,M)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal I$, there exists a bounded set $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)\subseteq {\mathbb R}^{|M|}$, such that eventually $U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\in B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$, for all ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$, where $U_{M,n} = X_n[M]'X_n[M]/n$. Here, $C>0$ is the constant from Condition~\ref{cond:X2}. Fix $(h,M)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal I$ and $t>0$, and define $g_h(t) = \sup_{|\gamma|>t} \min\{\phi_1(\gamma), \phi_2(\gamma)\}$ and the set $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$ by $$ B_{h,M}(\tau,C) = \{ v\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}: g_h(\|v\|/\sqrt{2}) \ge 2C[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)]/\tau\}, $$ where $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are as in Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:concave}. Note that, indeed, $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$ is bounded, because $g_h(t) \to -\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, in view of Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:cdf}. Next, fix $n$ large enough, such that Conditions~\ref{cond:X2}(\ref{cX2:rank},\ref{cX2:Huber}) hold. Then the pseudo parameter $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo} uniquely exists. For $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ and $\xi>0$, define $R_{\beta,n}(\xi) = \{ i\le n : |X_{i,n}[M]\beta|\ge \xi\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|\}$. Now fix $\xi>0$ and $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ such that $\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|=1$, and observe that \begin{align*} 1 \;&=\; \beta'X_n[M]'X_n[M]\beta/n \;=\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_{i,n}[M]U_{M,n}^{-1/2}U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta)^2 \\ &\le\; \xi^2 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i\in R_{\beta,n}(\xi)} \|U_{M,n}^{-1/2}X_{i,n}[M]'\|^2 \;\le\;\frac{1}{n} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| C \;+\; \xi^2, \end{align*} which implies that $\inf_{\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| = \inf_{\beta:\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|=1} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| \ge n(1-\xi^2)/C$. Since $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are negative, we get for every ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$, every $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ and for $\xi=1/\sqrt{2}$, that \begin{align*} {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot,\beta)] \;&\le\; \sum_{i\in R_{\beta,n}(\xi)} {\mathbb P}_{i,n}(\{1\}){\mathbb P}_{i,n}(\{0\}) \Big( \phi_1(X_{i,n}[M]\beta) + \phi_2(X_{i,n}[M]\beta)\Big)\\ &\le \; \tau \,|R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| \,g_h(\xi\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|) \;\le\; n \frac{\tau}{2C} g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|/\sqrt{2}), \end{align*} where $\mathbb M \triangleq (h,M)$. Therefore, we have $n[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)] \le {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot, 0)] \le {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot, \beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)] \le n \tau g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\|/\sqrt{2}) / (2C)$, which yields $$ g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\|/\sqrt{2}) \;\ge \; \frac{[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)] 2C}{\tau}, $$ i.e., $U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\in B_{h,M}(\tau, C)$. So we have established the preliminary result. Since the bounded set $B_{h,M}(\tau, C)$ depends only on the indicated quantities, there exists a finite positive constant $K^*_{h,M}(\tau, C)$, depending on the same quantities, such that for all large $n$, for all ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$ and for all $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$, \begin{align*} &\max_{i}|X_{i,n}[M]\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)| \le \max_i \|U_{M,n}^{-1/2}X_{i,n}[M]'\| \|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\|\\ &\quad\le \sqrt{C}K_{h,M}^*(\tau, C) \le \max_{(h,M)\in\mathcal H\times \mathcal I}\sqrt{C}K_{h,M}^*(\tau, C) =:K^*(\tau, C). \end{align*} This finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Show the standardized pseudo-parameter lies in a bounded set by comparing the expected log-likelihood at $0$ and at the maximizer.

nodes.name: Define $B_{h,M}$
nodes.statement: Fix $(h,M)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal I$ and $t>0$, and define $g_h(t) = \sup_{|\gamma|>t} \min\{\phi_1(\gamma), \phi_2(\gamma)\}$ and the set $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$ by $$ B_{h,M}(\tau,C) = \{ v\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}: g_h(\|v\|/\sqrt{2}) \ge 2C[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)]/\tau\}, $$ where $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are as in Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:concave}. Note that, indeed, $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$ is bounded, because $g_h(t) \to -\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, in view of Condition~\ref{cond:H}\eqref{cH:cdf}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $g_h$ and the bounded set $B_{h,M}(\tau,C)$.

nodes.name: Counting large predictors
nodes.statement: Next, fix $n$ large enough, such that Conditions~\ref{cond:X2}(\ref{cX2:rank},\ref{cX2:Huber}) hold. Then the pseudo parameter $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo} uniquely exists. For $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ and $\xi>0$, define $R_{\beta,n}(\xi) = \{ i\le n : |X_{i,n}[M]\beta|\ge \xi\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|\}$. Now fix $\xi>0$ and $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ such that $\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|=1$, and observe that \begin{align*} 1 \;&=\; \beta'X_n[M]'X_n[M]\beta/n \;=\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_{i,n}[M]U_{M,n}^{-1/2}U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta)^2 \\ &\le\; \xi^2 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i\in R_{\beta,n}(\xi)} \|U_{M,n}^{-1/2}X_{i,n}[M]'\|^2 \;\le\;\frac{1}{n} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| C \;+\; \xi^2, \end{align*} which implies that $\inf_{\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| = \inf_{\beta:\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|=1} |R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| \ge n(1-\xi^2)/C$.
nodes.statement_short: Many indices have large linear predictor: $|R_{\beta,n}(\xi)|\ge n(1-\xi^2)/C$.

nodes.name: Likelihood upper bound
nodes.statement: Since $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are negative, we get for every ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$, every $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{|M|}$ and for $\xi=1/\sqrt{2}$, that \begin{align*} {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot,\beta)] \;&\le\; \sum_{i\in R_{\beta,n}(\xi)} {\mathbb P}_{i,n}(\{1\}){\mathbb P}_{i,n}(\{0\}) \Big( \phi_1(X_{i,n}[M]\beta) + \phi_2(X_{i,n}[M]\beta)\Big)\\ &\le \; \tau \,|R_{\beta,n}(\xi)| \,g_h(\xi\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|) \;\le\; n \frac{\tau}{2C} g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta\|/\sqrt{2}), \end{align*} where $\mathbb M \triangleq (h,M)$.

nodes.name: Membership
nodes.statement: Therefore, we have $n[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)] \le {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot, 0)] \le {\mathbb E}_n[\ell_{\mathbb M,n}(\cdot, \beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)] \le n \tau g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\|/\sqrt{2}) / (2C)$, which yields $$ g_h(\|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*\|/\sqrt{2}) \;\ge \; \frac{[\phi_1(0) + \phi_2(0)] 2C}{\tau}, $$ i.e., $U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\in B_{h,M}(\tau, C)$. nodes.statement_short: Compare with $\beta=0$ to get membership in $B_{h,M}$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since the bounded set $B_{h,M}(\tau, C)$ depends only on the indicated quantities, there exists a finite positive constant $K^*_{h,M}(\tau, C)$, depending on the same quantities, such that for all large $n$, for all ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$ and for all $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$, \begin{align*} &\max_{i}|X_{i,n}[M]\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)| \le \max_i \|U_{M,n}^{-1/2}X_{i,n}[M]'\| \|U_{M,n}^{1/2}\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)\|\\ &\quad\le \sqrt{C}K_{h,M}^*(\tau, C) \le \max_{(h,M)\in\mathcal H\times \mathcal I}\sqrt{C}K_{h,M}^*(\tau, C) =:K^*(\tau, C). \end{align*} This finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded set and leverage bound give the uniform constant $K^*(\tau,C)$.

nodes.name: Bounds and continuity of the Hessian at the pseudo-parameter
nodes.statement: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond:X2}(\ref{cX2:rank},\ref{cX2:Huber}) and \ref{cond:H}(\ref{cH:cdf},\ref{cH:concave},\ref{cH:C2}) hold and fix $\tau\in(0,1/4)$. \begin{list}{(\roman{rcnt})}{ \usecounter{rcnt} \setlength\itemindent{0pt} \setlength\leftmargin{0pt} \setlength\partopsep{0pt} } \item There exist positive constants $\overline{K}(\tau, C)$ and $\underline{K}(\tau, C)$, depending only on $\tau$ and the constant $C$ from Condition~\ref{cond:X2}\eqref{cX2:Huber}, such that for all sufficiently large $n\in{\mathbb N}$, for all $\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n$, all ${\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)$ and all $y\in\{0,1\}^n$, \begin{align*} \overline{K}(\tau, C) &\ge \lambda_{\max}\left((X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{-1/2}H_{\mathbb M,n}^*(y)(X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{-1/2}\right)\\ &\ge\lambda_{\min}\left((X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{-1/2}H_{\mathbb M,n}^*(y)(X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{-1/2}\right) \ge \underline{K}(\tau, C), \end{align*} where $H_{\mathbb M,n}^*(y) := H_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n))$, $H_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta) = -\frac{\partial^2 \ell_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta)}{\partial\beta\partial\beta'}$ with $\beta\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)}$ and $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)$ is the pseudo parameter of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo}. \item For $\delta>0$ and $n$ sufficiently large, such that the pseudo parameter $\beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:pseudo} exists, define $$ N_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n}(\delta) = \left\{ \beta\in{\mathbb R}^{m(\mathbb M)} : \left\| (X_n[M]'X_n[M])^{1/2}(\beta - \beta_{\mathbb M,n}^*({\mathbb P}_n)) \right\| \le \delta\right\}. $$ Then, for every $\delta>0$, $$ \sup_{\substack{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n\\{\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{(\mathrm{bin})}(\tau)}} \sup_{y\in\{0,1\}^n}\sup_{\beta\in N_{\mathbb M,{\mathbb P}_n,n}(\delta)} \left\| H_{\mathbb M,n}^*(y)^{-1/2}H_{\mathbb M,n}(y,\beta)H_{\mathbb M,n}^*(y)^{-1/2} - I_{m(\mathbb M)} \right\| $$ converges to zero as $n\to\infty$. \item Suppose that, in addition, also Condition~\ref{cond:X2}\eqref{cX2:eigen} holds. Then there exists a positive finite constant $K(\tau, C)$, depending only on $\tau$ and the constant $C$ from Condition~\ref{cond:X2}, such that eventually $$ \sup_{\mathbb M\in\mathsf{M}_n}\sup_{{\mathbb P}_n\in\mathbf{P}_n^{\mathrm{(bin)}}(\tau)}\frac{\lambda_{\max}({\mathbb E}_{{\mathbb P}_n}[H_{\mathbb M,n}^*])}{\lambda_{\min}({\mathbb E}_{{\mathbb P}_n}[H_{\mathbb M,n}^*])} \;\le\; K(\tau, C). $$ \end{list}

conclusions: There exist positive constants $\overline{K}(\tau, C)$ and $\underline{K}(\tau, C)$
